articles.title: Why most journalists are tired of fact-checking Donald Trump
articles.summary: Journalists are abandoning basic fact-checking and overlooking major stories as President Trump’s provocative remarks dominate the news cycle.
articles.body: As I look at a decade of coverage of the man who loves all things gold, I have to conclude that many journalists are suffering from Trump Exhaustion Syndrome. It’s not about being physically tired, and of course there are exceptions. No, the syndrome involves throwing up your hands and abandoning basic fact-checking because, you know, they think, what the hell, everyone knows Trump says lots and lots of things that are untrue. Much of this is tied to the surge in social media. After all, why do a second-day story analyzing what the president did or said when the hot story is Trump praising Nicki Minaj and her beautiful butt? As for the truth-squadding part, don’t worry, I have the receipts. The other day, the president came out and said he had ordered the Justice Department to intervene in the crazy Alaska election. It was right there. He didn’t hide it. Pronounced it out in the open. I know the widespread belief that the department was doing his bidding — charging James Comey a third time? For younger readers, there used to be a brick wall between the White House and DOJ. If Joe Biden had breached that wall only once, he would have been impeached, convicted and behind bars. As a former Justice Department reporter, I can tell you that divide hasn’t been pulverized since Watergate, when AG John Mitchell went to prison. NOT EVEN SKY HIGH GAS PRICES OR THE IRAN WAR WILL STOP TRUMP SUPPORTERS VOTING MAGA Now a couple of the Sunday hosts, CNN’s Dana Bash and CBS’s Margaret Brennan, aggressively pressed Attorney General Todd Blanche about the controversy (two Dan Sullivans, and as the New York Times disclosed, the second guy was recruited by the Democrats). At one point, Blanche addressed the president’s order that his department file a lawsuit. "No, no, he didn’t say it on camera," the AG insisted. "Yes he did," Brennan shot back. Indeed, he did. But as I looked at the major papers the next day, the press had moved on. (My apologies if I missed someone’s brilliant analysis). It was as if the story no longer existed. That’s Trump Exhaustion Syndrome in action. Here’s another example. Just a couple of days ago, Trump said that while he might move the press briefing room, "the old swimming pool will never be brought back. I NEVER even thought of doing such a stupid thing!" That didn’t sound right to me, and boy was I exhausted after 20 seconds of fact-checking. People Magazine, just last month: "As President Donald Trump fights in court to ban particular news organizations from the White House, he suggested converting the White House press briefing room back to the indoor pool built during Franklin Delano Roosevelt’s tenure in ‘The People’s House.’" So we have a new definition of fake news: something the president used to say but has since changed his view and no longer stands by his previous position. Embed: I want to make something clear: I am not anti-Trump. I like him personally. I’ve covered him on and off since 1987, and interviewed him six times during the 2024 campaign. He can definitely be a charming guy in person. Most of the time, we’ve gotten along fine — he’s sent me a number of favorable notes — and sometimes, as is typical with him, not so much. There’s a reason half the country voted for him, even if many are now unhappy about the Iran war and rising prices at the pump. My goal here is to write about press behavior. Trump is a master media manipulator. He has known, since I was in New York writing about his exploits as a combative developer, how to distract the press from an unfavorable story, and he’s acknowledged as much to me. When the president says "Norway sucks" and is a "s***-house country" (because he’s still ticked off about not winning the Nobel Peace Prize), he knows it will make news. Same with his comments about Nicki Minaj’s anatomy. He understands most of the press will take the bait. Oh, and sometimes Trump just gets carried away at rallies. I’m not saying these things don’t deserve a mention in a feature column or as a cable-show kicker, but they do tend to squeeze out other stories. SOCIAL MEDIA EXPLODES WITH MEMES CELEBRATING TRUMP VICTORY When Trump called Barack Obama "stupid"— over a joke that the White House looks like Saddam’s Cheesecake Factory — he was edging into real news. And when he ordered the raid on Ilhan Omar’s home — abandoning the longstanding justice practice of doing nothing to influence politics in a campaign’s last 60 days — Trump created a major, important news story, no question about it. Back in 1987, Trump told me, without being asked, that if he ran for president, he would win. I confess to having been skeptical. CLICK HERE TO GET THE FOX NEWS APP After Trump came down the escalator in 2015, he told me he had a 15 to 20 percent chance of winning the nomination. He can be surprisingly candid. All these years later, it’s impossible to deny there’s a strong anti-Trump element in the media. By convincing themselves there’s no point in challenging him because he constantly lies, many are indeed suffering from Trump Exhaustion Syndrome.

articles.title: A California couple bought a home with a 20-by-20-foot garden, then a neighbour claimed the land; a 1955 deal involving $250 and babysitting helped secure their exclusive gardening rights in an October 26 ruling
articles.summary: A small garden became the centre of a legal battle between two California couples after a property survey revealed that the land belonged to a
articles.body: A small garden became the centre of a legal battle between two California couples after a property survey revealed that the land belonged to a neighbouring house. Rupert Clayton and Miriam Pinchuk had bought their Oakland home in 2019 believing that the 20-by-20-foot garden was included in the property. But their neighbours, Herbert Canada and Bernadette Rodriguez, claimed the land was legally theirs. The dispute eventually reached the California Court of Appeal, which ruled on Monday that Clayton and Pinchuk could continue using the garden exclusively.According to the California Judicial Branch, the disagreement was unusual because the garden had been separated from the neighbouring property for decades. A retaining wall and fence stood between the two homes, making the disputed area appear to be part of Clayton and Pinchuk's backyard. Thick vegetation also made it difficult to access the garden from the other property.When the couple bought their house, the garden was already well maintained. They considered it an important part of their new home and began using it regularly.However, the confusion had begun long before either couple moved into the neighbourhood. The answer to why the garden was enclosed within one property but legally belonged to another lay in an agreement made in 1955.A garage, $250 and a babysitting arrangementIn the 1950s, the two properties belonged to the Reom and Kroeger families. The Kroegers wanted to replace their garage, but their plans would interfere with an alleyway that the Reoms had the right to use.The families eventually reached an arrangement that allowed the construction to go ahead. The Reoms agreed to surrender their alleyway access rights, while the Kroegers agreed to give them a small section of land.The agreement also involved a payment of $250 and babysitting services provided by Carol Reom for the Kroegers' young child.Following the arrangement, the Kroegers built their new garage and put up a retaining wall and fence. The small piece of land was enclosed within the Reom family's backyard, where it remained for decades.Harry and Carol Reom continued using the area as a garden for more than 50 years. But although the two families had reached an agreement, the necessary property records were never properly completed, according to the findings later examined in court.That missing paperwork became important when the houses changed hands and the new owners began questioning where one property ended and the other began.How new neighbours became involvedCanada and Rodriguez purchased the Piedmont property in 2017. Two years later, Clayton and Pinchuk bought the adjoining Oakland house from the Reom family trust.Before the second sale, however, Canada had already been in contact with the Reom family over a separate matter.In 2018, he needed permission to connect to a drainage pipe on their property for renovation work. During those discussions, Larry Reom, the son of Harry and Carol, told him about the old land agreement and provided a document describing it.Larry later testified that Canada had indicated he would have the document officially recorded. The Reom family subsequently allowed the drainage connection without asking for payment.The garden issue came up again in 2020, when Clayton and Pinchuk discussed replacing the boundary fence with their neighbours. Canada showed them a survey indicating that the garden was legally part of his property.This came as a surprise to the couple, who had believed that the garden was included in their purchase.The disagreement continued until December 2021, when Canada contacted the police and reported that Clayton and Pinchuk were trespassing. The couple stopped using the garden while they pursued the matter in court.What the court discovered By the time the case went to trial, the people who had made the original arrangement in 1955 were no longer available to explain what had happened. The court therefore had to rely on surviving documents and testimony from family members.Larry Reom said he had seen a written record of the agreement among his parents' papers, but he could not locate it when the case was heard. Other documents, including old correspondence, supported the account that the families had agreed to exchange the garden area for money, babysitting, and the surrender of alleyway access rights.The court also considered how the land had been used since the 1950s. The Reom family had maintained the garden for decades, while the wall and fence had kept it physically separate from the Kroeger property.After hearing the evidence, the trial court decided that Clayton and Pinchuk should be allowed to continue gardening there, even though it could not establish that ownership of the land had been legally transferred.It granted them an equitable easement, a legal right allowing someone to use another person's land for a particular purpose without owning it.Why Canada and Rodriguez lost appealCanada and Rodriguez challenged the trial court's decision, arguing that the couple should not have been given exclusive gardening rights over land that legally belonged to them.The appeal required the judges to consider whether allowing Clayton and Pinchuk to keep using the garden would be fair, given the history of the two properties.One important consideration was how much the couple stood to lose. They had bought their home believing that the garden was included and had spent two years developing it. The area also had fertile soil and was among the flattest parts of their backyard.The court found that Canada and Rodriguez had made little use of the disputed land. Their drainage needs had also been addressed through the separate permission granted by the Reom family.The judges considered the 1955 arrangement particularly important because the previous owners of the neighbouring property had already benefited from it by being able to build their garage. The appellate court ultimately agreed with the trial court's assessment and upheld its decision.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: In 2014, demolition work next door damaged a Miami woman's home, but her insurer said the policy excluded the loss; 12 years later, a Florida appeals court upheld her victory over the insurer
articles.summary: What happens when construction work on a neighbouring property damages a home, but the homeowner's insurance company refuses to pay for repairs?
articles.body: What happens when construction work on a neighbouring property damages a home, but the homeowner's insurance company refuses to pay for repairs? For Sandra Moise of Miami, Florida, the dispute centred on whether vibrations from demolition work could be excluded under policy provisions covering earth movement and settlement. The damage occurred in March 2014, and the insurer denied her claim that June, setting off a legal battle that continued for years.On October 28, 2026, Florida's Third District Court of Appeal upheld the judgment in Moise's favour against Homeowners Choice Property & Casualty Insurance Company. In its opinion available on Justia, the court concluded that the insurer had not established grounds to overturn the jury's decision. The ruling affirmed a $240,000 damages award, along with prejudgment interest, and addressed the distinction between damage caused by vibrations and damage resulting from actual earth movement.Demolition vibrations damaged the homeAccording to the court's opinion, Moise's home was insured under a policy that took effect on May 8, 2013. On March 1, 2014, demolition activity at a neighbouring property allegedly caused vibrations that damaged the house's floors, walls and ceiling. Moise said she was inside the property during the demolition and felt the shaking. She also noticed picture frames moving and later discovered damage to the house. Her initial complaint, filed on August 27, 2014, alleged that the insurer had failed to cover the loss.Homeowners Choice arranged an inspection by Bracken Engineering, which examined the property on May 6, 2014. The insurer's field adjuster inspected it later that month. The company subsequently denied the claim on June 6, 2014, concluding that the damage resulted from material shrinkage or settlement and fell within the policy's exclusions.Insurer cited earth movement and settlement exclusionsThe insurance policy covered direct physical losses occurring during the policy period, subject to its exclusions. These included damage caused by earthquakes, landslides, sinking or shifting earth, soil expansion or contraction, and the settling or cracking of foundations. The company argued that the damage to Moise's home fell within these provisions. It maintained that the cracks and other problems were attributable to settlement or pre-existing conditions rather than vibrations alone.Moise's expert, Alfredo Brizuela, offered a different explanation. His report stated that the impact of heavy construction equipment at the adjacent property generated vibrations that travelled through the limestone subsoil and affected the home's foundation structure. In an affidavit, Brizuela clarified that the damage resulted from vibrations, rather than actual displacement or movement of the earth. This distinction became central to the dispute because the court distinguished damage caused by vibrations without actual earth movement from damage resulting from earth movement or settlement covered by the policy's exclusions.The trial court denied the insurer's request for summary judgment on the exclusion issue in December 2019. It subsequently restricted certain arguments about whether vibration itself constituted an excluded cause of loss. The case went to a jury trial in November 2022, and the jury found that the damage was not excluded under the policy. Final judgment was entered on May 1, 2024.Appeals court explains why the exclusions did not apply automaticallyHomeowners Choice challenged the outcome, arguing that the trial court had wrongly interpreted the policy and restricted evidence relevant to its defence. The Third District Court of Appeal rejected the insurer's arguments. The appellate court considered earlier decisions involving similar insurance provisions. It distinguished cases in which damage resulted from actual earth movement from those in which vibrations or shock waves caused damage without accompanying movement of the earth.The judges noted that the parties had presented conflicting expert evidence. While the insurer's expert attributed the damage to settlement or other conditions, Moise's expert maintained that vibrations alone had caused it. That conflict did not justify overturning the jury's verdict. The court also found no demonstrated prejudice from the trial court's evidentiary rulings. The insurer had been able to present its position that settlement, rather than vibration, caused the damage. Its expert testified at trial that, although vibrations had occurred, they had not caused the damage. The appeals court therefore found no basis to reverse the judgment on these grounds.Court upholds $240,000 award and prejudgment interestThe insurer also challenged the monetary award, arguing that the operative complaint was framed as a declaratory judgment action and that the trial court had improperly awarded damages. The appellate court disagreed. It noted that Moise's complaint had also sought monetary damages attributable to the loss if the damage was covered. Florida law permits further relief based on a declaratory judgment when necessary or appropriate.The jury had determined damages of $240,000, and the trial court had added prejudgment interest. The appeals court affirmed this part of the judgment as well, upholding the orders under review in all respects. The ruling does not mean that every property damage claim involving construction vibrations must be covered by insurance. Instead, it highlights the importance of establishing the actual cause of damage and examining the precise wording of policy exclusions. In Moise's case, the court upheld the jury's determination that the damage was not excluded under the policy, affirming the judgment in her favour.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: ‘I held this woman in my arms. She died’: Spain mourns train crash victims
articles.summary: Second tragedy on line in about nine months raises questions about levels of investment in railway maintenance.
articles.body:
Madrid, Spain – Joaquim Torres, who was travelling on a train which crashed into another on Wednesday, rushed to help his fellow passengers who had been injured.

Fighting back tears, he told Al Jazeera: “I held this woman in my arms and tried to comfort her, but she stopped breathing. She died, she died.”

One of about 500 passengers caught in the deadly crash, Torres had been travelling on a high-speed train from the capital, Madrid, to Seville in the south of the country. All seemed normal, until the huge crash just before 9am.

At least 68 people were killed and 77 others were injured.

Spain’s national train operator Renfe has launched an investigation into the disaster, which happened in a rural area between Urda and Los Yebenes, two small towns south of Toledo in central Spain.

But the disaster has renewed a national debate over whether Spain’s high-speed train network is safe, nine months after another train crash on the same line in which 46 people died and scores were injured at Adamuz, near Cordoba in southern Spain.

Sebastian Herrero, a 46-year-old doctor who was on the train, described the scene after Wednesday’s collision.

“There were three train carriages from which they kept pulling people out and covering them with sheets. Bodies. It’s apocalyptic. It’s hard to imagine that anyone could still be alive in those three carriages. It’s a twisted mass of metal. It’s as if a bomb had gone off,” he told Al Jazeera.

Rescuers searched for survivors through the mangled wreckage of three carriages at the front of the train, which had smashed into a stationary locomotive.

Desperate relatives were waiting at Seville train station holding pictures of loved ones who had failed to arrive in the southern city, as Spanish TV presenters, dressed in black, reported on the tragedy.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, who has declared three days of national mourning, said: “All of Spain is mourning,” before adding that it is “not acceptable for a country like Spain” to have two major train disasters in one year. A judicial investigation is expected to begin shortly.

Spain’s Transport Minister Oscar Puente said the deadly crash happened after a Renfe train was authorised to continue on its journey – despite an active red signal because of a stationary train on the line ahead, operated by the Italian consortium Iryo.

Puente said the red signal had been issued due to a computer communications failure which automatically stopped traffic, and an “inexplicable” order from the central command centre was given for the Renfe train to move on. He said train engineers were not to blame.

The trade union Solidarity, which is linked to Spain’s far-right Vox party, held a demonstration in Madrid on Wednesday night to demand Puente’s resignation, and riot police were dispatched.

In the wake of the crash, Alberto Nunez Feijoo, leader of the opposition conservative People’s Party, which is favourite to win the upcoming general election, told reporters: “Spain has the right to know what is happening with its infrastructure, the condition of the tracks and safety systems, what warnings were received from Adamuz and measures were taken.

“The Spanish people have a right to a complete and independent review of the entire rail network.”

Fernando Seco, another passenger in the Renfe train bound for Seville, said the train had just resumed its journey following a brief stop when it collided with the other train.

“We felt a brutal crash. People were thrown through the air, seats were flying through the air,” he told TVE state television.

After leaving the wrecked train, he said he saw a “carriage split in half, with dead people trapped inside”.

Once news of the crash got out, volunteers rushed to the scene to offer whatever help they could give.

Jose Maria Rabadan, a resident of Urda, the closest town, said he and other volunteers brought food, water and blankets and provided transport for those affected by the crash.

“Whatever they ask of us, we will bring,” he told Radio Castilla-La Mancha.

The rail accident is likely to come as a major blow to the ruling Socialist Party, just a month before the country goes to the polls in a general election on November 29.

The government’s management of the Adamuz rail crash in January was heavily criticised by opposition politicians and raised questions about the levels of investment in railway maintenance in recent years.

Rail unions had planned a strike for Thursday to protest about what they say is a poor safety record on the Spanish network.

The tragedy also comes amid a boom in the use of high-speed trains, which has not been accompanied by necessary investment in maintenance of the high-speed network, according to European Commission data.

The number of rail accidents, including collisions and derailments, rose from 45 in 2016 to 57 in 2024, and surged to 69 in 2025, according to the Spanish railway safety authority (AESF).

Some 40 million people used the high-speed rail trains in 2024, almost double the figure for 2019. However, in the first half of this year, about 25 million travelled on the high-speed network, a year-on-year fall of 14 percent.

With cheaper fares compared with many other developed countries, the high-speed rail network has been seen as an achievement for Spain in recent years, with its expertise exported to Saudi Arabia and the United Kingdom.

Between 2018 and 2022, Spain spent an average of about $1.67bn each year on high-speed lines, more than other countries with similar networks. However, only 16 percent of that was spent on maintenance or repairs, with the rest going on infrastructure, according to EC figures.

By contrast, Italy, Germany and France spent on average between 33 and 39 percent of their budgets on maintenance, even though each country has much smaller networks than the 4,000km (2,485 miles) in Spain.

Experts say the success of the Spanish high-speed network is putting safety at risk.

“The problem is that the train network has become very popular as it is cheap and accessible but the authorities have not spent enough on its maintenance in recent years,” Salvador Garcia-Ayllon, a professor at the Universidad Politecnica in Cartagena, who specialises in civil engineering, told Al Jazeera.

Following the Adamuz disaster, a preliminary investigation found a rail fracture was the cause of the crash, but an ongoing investigation by police has not been concluded. A judicial investigation is now expected.

articles.title: Ethiopia receives 12 Russian fighter jets and air defence systems as Tigray war escalates
articles.summary: The acquisition of the warplanes comes amid ongoing fighting in northern Tigray region that started last month.
articles.body:
Ethiopia has received 12 Su-35 fighter jets from Russia, as fighting intensified in the northern Tigray region neighbouring Eritrea.

Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, who is attending the Russia-Africa summit in Moscow, described the acquisition as a "milestone" that would boost Ethiopia's defence capacity.

He said Ethiopia and Russia agreed on the deal several years ago and the warplanes had come ahead of schedule. He also said that Ethiopia had plans to acquire four S-400 air defence systems from Moscow.

The Ethiopian leader said the military hardware was essential to protect the country from external threats.

Abiy, who described Russian President Vladimir Putin, "as a close friend of Ethiopia", said Ethiopia had now become the first country in sub‑Saharan Africa to own this kind of "advanced combat technology."

"If we fail to build this capability, surviving as a country in our region will become difficult. Countries with sufficient preparation are not easily defied," he said.

Russia and Ethiopia have signed several military agreements in recent years, including a deal in 2021 to train and improve technology for the military.

Abiy explained that Ethiopia signed an agreement with Russia several years ago to procure the Su‑35 jets and S‑400 systems, citing global air force trends and security threats facing the country.

The Su‑35, he noted, is equipped for both air‑to‑air and air‑to‑ground combat, with the ability to detect and neutralize incoming cruise missiles at distances of up to 200 kilometers.

Military intelligence analyst Qalaab Segatu told BBC Amharic that Ethiopia's acquisition of additional warplanes was a key indication that "it was preparing for possible wars with other countries, not just internal conflicts".

According to him, the jets are highly maneuverable and capable of covering large areas, with radars capable of ensuring air superiority and long-range scanning.

When combined, the fighter jets and air defence systems "create a significant capability to protect and defend major cities and critical infrastructure such as the Renaissance Dam, providing key strategic air superiority," Qalaab said.

Abiy said besides the advanced capabilities of the aircraft from Russia, the use of drones was equally important in strengthening deterrence.

Ethiopia has extensively used military drones, including those sourced from Turkey and China, in recent conflicts.

"We need to build capacity not only with drones, but also with the fourth generation capabilities of the Su 30 and Su 35 [aircraft]," Abiy said.

The latest acquisition of military hardware from Russia comes after the current conflict in northern Tigray started last month between the government and the party that controls Tigray, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF).

Both blame each other for violating a 2022 deal that ended a civil war.

Ethiopia accuses Eritrea of backing the TPLF, which it denies.

Tensions between the two countries have also persisted as Abiy terms Ethiopia's lack of direct sea access an "existential question", which Eritrea views as a direct threat to its sovereignty.

Eritrea gained independence in 1993 after a decades-long war with Ethiopia, with the latter losing access to the sea.

articles.title: A Minnesota lake boundary battle dating to 2017 takes a new turn as an appeals court backs a trust's access to Prairie Lake and upholds a ruling that wiped out neighbours' earlier $148,500 trespass award
articles.summary: A dispute between neighbours over access to a lake in Minnesota has taken another turn after nearly nine years in court.
articles.body: A dispute between neighbours over access to a lake in Minnesota has taken another turn after nearly nine years in court. On Monday, the Minnesota Court of Appeals ruled in favour of the Blackwood Trust, confirming that its property has direct access to Prairie Lake in St. Louis County. The decision is a setback for neighbours Vicky Jo Ulvestad and Lawrence Craig Hammonds, who had earlier won $148,500 after accusing the trust of entering their land without permission. That award has now been cancelled.According to the court judgment, the disagreement began over where one property ends and the other begin. Ulvestad and Hammonds own a piece of land known as Lot 3, while the Blackwood Trust owns the neighbouring Lots 4 and 5. Both sides disagreed over whether Lot 4 reached the lake or whether a portion of Lot 3 stood in its way.What made the matter more confusing was that two surveys of the land gave different answers. A survey carried out in 1997 showed that Lot 4 did not reach Prairie Lake. However, when the same surveyor examined the properties again in 2010, he reached a different conclusion. The newer survey showed that Lot 4 did have access to the lake.After the 2010 survey, the trust built a cabin on its property. Over the next few years, trees were removed, and a path was created through an area that the neighbours believed belonged to them. The disagreement eventually became a legal battle in 2017. The trust initially asked the court for permission to cross Lot 3 to reach the lake. Ulvestad and Hammonds, meanwhile, accused the trust of trespassing and wanted it stopped from entering their land or removing more trees.How Ulvestad and Hammonds initially won At first, the court sided with Ulvestad and Hammonds. It accepted their understanding of where the property boundary lay and decided that Lot 4 did not have direct access to Prairie Lake.The neighbours also won their claim that the trust had entered their property without permission. A jury awarded them $49,400, and the court later increased the amount to $148,500.But the dispute did not end there. The trust challenged the decision, maintaining that its land extended all the way to the lake.In December 2024, the Minnesota Court of Appeals found that an important piece of evidence had not been properly considered. It was an old government map from 1870 showing how the land around Prairie Lake had originally been divided.The appeals court asked the lower court to examine this map before deciding the boundary again. This gave the trust another opportunity to establish that its property reached the water.How an old map changed the outcomeThe 1870 map became important because it showed the original layout of the properties surrounding Prairie Lake.It also contained lines showing the lake's shoreline at the time. These are known as meander lines, which show where the water was when the land was first surveyed.However, the shoreline of a lake can change over time. This means the line drawn on an old map does not always mark the exact boundary of a property today. As explained in the court proceedings, landowners whose properties reach a lake can also own the land between the old survey line and the water's edge.To understand where the properties should meet the lake, a surveyor working for the trust studied the historic map and prepared a fresh survey in April 2025.He used a method called the long-lake method, which takes the shape of a lake into account when deciding how the boundaries of neighbouring properties should be drawn. The new survey supported the trust's claim that Lot 4 reached Prairie Lake without crossing Lot 3.After considering the evidence, the lower court accepted the new boundary. It ruled that the trust's property had its own access to the lake. As a result, the neighbours' trespass claims were dismissed, and the earlier $148,500 award was cancelled.Neighbours challenged the decision againUlvestad and Hammonds disagreed with the new ruling and returned to the appeals court. They argued that the boundary should have been decided using the original 1870 map rather than relying on the survey prepared in 2025. They believed the southern boundary of their property continued in a straight line towards the lake.They also raised concerns about the surveyor whose findings had helped the trust. During the earlier proceedings, the lower court had initially restricted what evidence could be presented. It later allowed additional testimony from the surveyor.The neighbours said this change had left them without a fair opportunity to challenge his findings. They raised another objection as well. An earlier survey supporting their position had been prepared by the former owner of the same surveying company. They questioned how surveys from the same company could reach different conclusions.However, the appeals court did not accept these arguments. The judges found that the neighbours had been given opportunities to present evidence against the surveyor's findings but had not shown how that evidence might have changed the result.The court also found no sufficient reason to prevent the surveyor from giving evidence simply because an earlier survey from the same company had reached a different conclusion.You use AI every day. articles.title: DR MARC SIEGEL: America’s awful marijuana addiction is spreading from parents to kids
articles.summary: A new study reveals approximately 6 million children live with a parent who uses cannabis most days, as THC content in products has surged dramatically.
articles.body: Marijuana is becoming the new alcohol — or worse. And children are paying the price. Not only is cannabis use skyrocketing in this country, with close to 70 million users every year, but parents are increasingly subjecting their children to wafting, intoxicating smoke. A new study from the University of California San Diego, a school based in a state with a big marijuana problem, shows that nationwide approximately 6 million children are living with a parent who uses cannabis most days. MARIJUANA USE RISES SHARPLY AMONG ONE GROUP OF AMERICANS, NEW STUDY FINDS As I pointed out on "The Ingraham Angle" recently (both host Laura Ingraham and I are highly concerned about the impact of chronic marijuana use), children are twice as likely to use cannabis themselves if they live in a household where a parent is a regular user, according to the National Survey on Drug Use and Health. Cannabis use has more than doubled in the adult population over the past two decades (it’s now over 8%), according to data from the National Center for Biotechnology Information. MARIJUANA USERS MAY FACE HIDDEN DRIVING DANGER THAT STANDARD TESTS CAN MISS Cannabis is highly addictive, and the THC content has increased greatly in all its forms, making it more and more dangerous. Edibles now typically contain up to 10 mg THC per serving, and concentrates and vape cartridges contain 50% to 95% THC (the psychoactive chemical in cannabis). The buds and flowers used for joints, vapes, edibles and concentrates are now 15 to 25% THC — a few decades ago, the amount was just 1 to 2%. Children are the victims here, and the impact starts as early as the womb. Fetal exposure leads to nearly twice the risk of premature birth and a two-and-a-half-times-greater risk of being born underweight or needing immediate medical intervention in the Neonatal ICU. Yet national data shows that over 5% of pregnant women have used marijuana products over the past month, and the number is climbing. SHARON STONE'S TERRIFYING WEED WITHDRAWAL SPARKS WARNING ABOUT TODAY'S POTENT MARIJUANA Plus, if a child is exposed to marijuana in the womb, research shows that there is a 2.5 times greater risk of THC product use during the child’s early teen years. A landmark study from Harvard found that a mother’s cannabis use during a child’s first 12 years of life is linked to the child beginning to use marijuana by the age of 16. BRAD PITT SAYS HE CAN DRINK IN ‘RESTRAINED MANNER’ AFTER 7 SOBER YEARS, BUT EXPERT RAISES RED FLAG Regular marijuana use is not just addictive and contagious; it also directly impacts parenting. Parents who are regular users are more prone to emotional outbursts, car accidents, poor parenting, and mental health disorders. Regular cannabis use can also cause emotional dysregulation, mood swings, impaired judgment and unexpected outbursts of anger or irritability. Research shows that anxiety in parents leads directly to anxiety in children. Where do we go from here? Look to our long history with alcohol. Strategies developed and used over generations for dealing with another highly addictive substance, alcohol, can help parents develop the tools they need to help themselves and their children. articles.title: Poundland's future hangs in the balance as chain edges towards collapse
articles.summary: Poundland's bosses is filing a notice of intention to appoint administrators to the business.
articles.body:
The future of Poundland hangs in the balance as the discount chain edges towards collapse, the BBC understands.

The retailer's bosses are filing a notice of intention to appoint administrators, which if approved by the High Court, will give the business 10 days breathing space to find a rescue deal.

The move comes after Poundland's managing director Barry Williams wrote a memo to his 12,000 staff across its 600 stores in the UK and Ireland saying the chains' US owner had limited Poundland's access to funding.

It is understood the firm's owner, Gordon Brothers, wants to break up the firm, with rivals Poundstretcher, B&M and Lidl interested in potentially buying up stores.

Gordon Brothers bought Poundland, which had been struggling, from the Polish retail group Pepco in June last year for a nominal £1, but a little over a year later it put the business up for sale.

Irish firm Martin Property Group (MPG) put forward a bid to take the business on as a going concern, which was the preferred option for management, but it is understood this did not meet Gordon Brothers' expectations.

Gordon Brothers wants to recoup a £30m shareholder loan it inherited from the previous owners as part of a its deal, but it is understood the Martin Property Group offer was for £5m, with the rest of the payment deferred.

It means Poundland is now heading towards an insolvency process.

Gordon Brothers could secure a new owner through what is known as a pre-pack administration.

But the most likely option for the business to be broken up and for parcels of stores to be sold.

Poundland was founded in 1990 with a store in Burton-upon-Trent, and has around 20 million customers per year.

It sells low-cost everyday products, general merchandise and fashion on local high streets.

The curious case of why Poundland is struggling during a cost-of-living crisis

Poundland in rescue talks as owners seek buyer

A Gordon Brothers insider said breaking the firm up would allow creditors to recover more money, and that this process would ultimately offer the best outcome for staff. The US investment firm's position is that current employees may be able to get employment with new store owners.

If this type of insolvency happens, it would let interested parties firm up offers.

These include Poundstretcher owner, Fortress, which according to one insider is interested in taking on between 200 and 250 stores.

Another large retailer is understood to be interested in buying up more than 100 other sites.

More than half a dozen retailers, include Iceland, Lidl, and B&M, have expressed interest in Poundland's store estate.

However, there is a split between the owners and the management running Poundland, who described the situation as "unexpected, unwanted and wholly avoidable".

"As you all know, our sales are strong and our recovery is taking root. This business simply does not deserve to go into any kind of administration," the chain's managing director Williams said in a message to staff this week.

He revealed that Gordon Brothers had limited Poundland's access to funds which help it run its day-to-day business.

"I'm disappointed to have to tell you that Gordon Brothers have given instructions that restricts our access to funds that we would, in normal circumstances expect to access fully under our existing loan agreement," he added.

In the memo, seen by the BBC, Williams said the offer from Martin Property Group was a "fully funded, ready to go bid that would have kept the business intact and able to continue the remarkable progress we've made".

Three independent directors who were appointed earlier this month to help oversee a sale resigned with immediate effect after disagreeing with Gordon Brothers' decision not to accept MPG's solvent offer.

The BBC understands Gordon Brothers has lined up AlixPartners as administrators.

Gordon Brothers previously said while MPG was identified as the "preferred bidder" by Poundland's management team, "attention must now turn to other active bids".

"These options will now be objectively evaluated, with a view to minimising uncertainty for Poundland's people and all relevant stakeholders," it said.

articles.title: MLC election results: BJP wins big, but Congress and Samajwadi Party send a message from Nagpur, Varanasi
articles.summary: The MLC elections across four states brought both shock and cheer for the BJP and Congress.
articles.body: The MLC elections across four states brought both shock and cheer for the BJP and Congress. While the Congress suffered a humiliating defeat in Karnataka, where it is in power but failed to win a single seat, the BJP faltered in two constituencies which mattered the most. One being Nagpur, which is home to the RSS headquarters, and Varanasi, Prime Minister Narendra Modi's parliamentary constituency.The BJP nevertheless emerged as the largest party, winning 13 of the 28 seats contested, while its allies took the NDA's tally to 16. The alliance swept all four seats in Karnataka, won six of the 11 seats in Uttar Pradesh and secured four of the eight seats in Bihar. In Maharashtra, the ruling Mahayuti won two of the five seats, while the opposition Maha Vikas Aghadi secured three.The Congress's only victory came from Nagpur, a political stronghold of Maharashtra chief minister Devendra Fadnavis and Union minister Nitin Gadkari. In Uttar Pradesh, the Samajwadi Party retained the Varanasi Teachers' constituency and was heading towards victory in the Graduates' seat, both of which it had won in 2020.What began as celebrations and sharp jibes at the Congress on Wednesday turned into a war of words on Thursday, as the results in Nagpur and Varanasi gave the opposition grounds to question the BJP's claims of electoral dominance.BJP mocks Congress over 'zero' seatsAs the early results came in on Wednesday, BJP leaders targeted the Congress over its poor performance, particularly in Karnataka, where the party is in power but failed to win a single seat.PM Modi took a swipe at the opposition party on X, pointing out that voting in the four states had taken place using ballot papers."Guess how many seats Congress won?" he asked.The remark came amid the Congress's repeated allegations over electronic voting machines and its demand for a return to ballot-paper voting.BJP president Nitin Nabin also targeted the Congress, saying the party had failed to win public support despite voting being conducted using ballot papers."The people are repeatedly rejecting Congress' anarchist politics," Nabin said, adding that public trust remained with PM Modi irrespective of whether elections were conducted using EVMs or ballot papers.BJP spokesperson Sudhanshu Trivedi also attacked Rahul Gandhi over his allegations of vote theft"Kamchori ki aadat chhodiye. Vote chori ka shabd apke muh se khud chhoot jayega," he said, asking the Congress leader to give up what he described as a habit of avoiding hard work.Nagpur win gives Congress a chance to respondCongress candidate and sitting MLC Abhijeet Wanjari defeated BJP's Sudhakar Kohale to retain the Nagpur Division Graduates' constituency after more than 40 hours of counting.Kohale had initially taken the lead before Wanjari overtook him through preferential votes.Nagpur is important for the BJP. Besides housing the RSS headquarters, it is associated with Fadnavis and Gadkari, both of whom campaigned for Kohale.The Congress had wrested the seat from the BJP in 2020, when Wanjari defeated Sandip Joshi. By retaining it in 2026, the party prevented the BJP from reclaiming a constituency it had dominated for decades.The Maharashtra Congress also targeted Fadnavis over a social media post in which he had claimed that the party had failed to win a single seat.Sharing a screenshot of what it said was a deleted post by Fadnavis, the party accused him of celebrating before counting was complete. The post had described the Congress's performance as a "big fat zero".The Congress said Fadnavis had been forced to delete the post after the Nagpur result and warned that the outcome was only a trailer of future political battles.Congress general secretary Jairam Ramesh also responded to PM Modi's remarks, questioning the BJP's losses in Nagpur and Varanasi."The Prime Minister needs to introspect, but instead, he's lecturing others! Before counting Congress's seats, I wish he'd also reflect on why the BJP lost both seats in his own parliamentary constituency of Varanasi, and how Congress managed to defeat the BJP in RSS's stronghold of Nagpur?" Ramesh said."Mr. Modi, stop the trolling," he added, accusing the government of failing to address inflation, unemployment and weak private investment.Ramesh claimed that voters in Varanasi, Nagpur, Lucknow, Prayagraj and Patna had expressed dissatisfaction with the Centre's policies.Varanasi setback gives SP a boost ahead of 2027The BJP's biggest setback in Uttar Pradesh came from Varanasi, where the Samajwadi Party retained the Teachers' seat and established an unassailable lead in the Graduates' constituency.The BJP retained six of the 11 seats contested in the state, while the SP won four and was heading towards a fifth.The SP had won both Varanasi seats in 2020 as well. Six years later, the BJP has failed to dislodge the party from either constituency despite its strong presence in the region.Although the two MLC constituencies cover a wider geographical area than PM Modi's Lok Sabha seat, the results carry political significance given Varanasi's association with the Prime Minister since 2014.They also come after PM Modi's victory margin in Varanasi declined from nearly 4.8 lakh votes in the 2019 Lok Sabha elections to around 1.5 lakh in 2024.Across Uttar Pradesh, the SP's tally is set to rise from three seats in 2020 to five, while the BJP has retained its tally of six.The SP had also emerged as the largest party in Uttar Pradesh in the 2024 Lok Sabha elections, winning 37 of the state's 80 parliamentary seats against the BJP's 33.BJP deputy chief minister Keshav Prasad Maurya acknowledged that the party had expected a better performance."These elections are decided by highly educated and qualified voters. The BJP has repeated its previous performance, but we expected to win more seats. We will examine why we fell short," Maurya said.The SP, meanwhile, has repeatedly accused the BJP of electoral irregularities, allegations the ruling party has rejected.On polling day, Akhilesh Yadav had claimed that the BJP was attempting to influence even the MLC elections, which have a limited electorate."If the BJP can do this in MLC polls for teachers and graduate constituencies where a limited number of people cast votes, one can imagine their preparation for the assembly polls," he had said.What do the results mean for 2027?The NDA's overall tally shows that the BJP and its allies remain ahead in these Legislative Council contests. But the results in Nagpur and Varanasi also show that the party has struggled to regain certain seats despite its strong presence in both regions.In Uttar Pradesh, the SP and Congress are preparing to contest the 2027 assembly elections together, hoping to build on their performance in the 2024 Lok Sabha polls.(function(){function e(){window.addEventListener(message,function(e){if(e.data[datawrapper-height]!==void 0){var t=document.querySelectorAll(iframe);for(var n in e.data[datawrapper-height])for(var r=0,i;i=t[r];r++)if(i.contentWindow===e.source){var a=e.data[datawrapper-height][n]+px;i.style.height=a}}})}e()})();The alliance won 43 of the state's 80 parliamentary seats in 2024, reducing the BJP's tally from 62 in 2019 to 33. Akhilesh Yadav has said the alliance will continue in 2027, although the two parties still need to settle their seat-sharing arrangement.The MLC results, however, cannot be treated as an indication of how the state will vote in the assembly elections. These contests involve a limited electorate of registered graduates and teachers, unlike assembly polls, which are decided by a much wider voter base.For the BJP, which is seeking a third consecutive term in Uttar Pradesh, the challenge will be to counter the opposition's gains. articles.title: After losing her son to an electric shock on the family farm, a Bihar woman invested in solar irrigation; now Ladli Khatoon supplies water to 35 to 38 farmers and has earned around Rs 1 lakh
articles.summary: In Bahwanpur, Ghoncha village in Bihar’s Muzaffarpur district, Ladli Khatoon has turned a personal tragedy into an opportunity to build a more secure
articles.body: In Bahwanpur, Ghoncha village in Bihar’s Muzaffarpur district, Ladli Khatoon has turned a personal tragedy into an opportunity to build a more secure future for her family. After losing her son to an electric shock while he was helping irrigate their crops, she became acutely aware of the dangers farmers can face while working in the fields. Today, she runs a solar-powered irrigation business, supplying water to 35 to 38 farmers and earning around Rs 1 lakh.Her journey is part of a growing initiative in Bihar that is helping rural women become solar entrepreneurs. By using sunlight to power irrigation pumps, these women are not only helping farmers access water but also building independent sources of income in communities where women have traditionally faced barriers to running businesses.From personal tragedy to a new beginningLadli’s family once depended largely on her husband’s earnings as an autorickshaw driver. With six family members to support and 1.5 acres of agricultural land, managing household expenses was not easy. The death of her son during irrigation brought an unimaginable loss to the family. The incident also highlighted the risks associated with conventional irrigation methods and the importance of exploring alternatives. Ladli later learned about the solar irrigation initiative at a meeting organised through JEEViKA, Bihar’s rural livelihoods programme. She was associated with the Muskan Self-Help Group (SHG), the Dharti Mata Village Organisation and the Phoolmala Cluster Level Federation.The programme offered her a chance to establish an irrigation enterprise of her own. However, setting it up required a substantial financial commitment. The solar irrigation system cost Rs 4,92,275, of which Ladli invested Rs 1,79,420. She also took a loan of Rs 1,25,000 from Rang De, a social lending organisation. For a family already managing financial difficulties, investing such a significant amount was a major decision. Yet, Ladli moved forward, hoping the venture would give her a more reliable source of income. Her decision has since changed the way she sees herself and her future.“A lot has changed in my life. There used to be financial anxiety because we were entirely reliant on one source of income. I am also learning new things. I didn't know solar energy could be used for irrigation. I am making money now, too. I feel self-assured. I am respected by the villagers,” she says.How solar irrigation is creating rural entrepreneursLadli’s business is part of a broader model developed through a partnership involving JEEViKA, the Aga Khan Rural Support Programme (India) and the Gates Foundation. Under this initiative, women farmers are selected through Cluster Level Federations and receive support to establish solar-powered irrigation systems. The setup includes a five-horsepower solar pump, solar panels, a borewell, a pipeline and a pump house. Self-help groups and village organisations can also help women access loans when they need financial assistance.The women then supply irrigation water to other farmers, creating a business around an essential agricultural service. Unlike systems that depend on conventional electricity or diesel, solar-powered pumps use sunlight as their energy source, potentially reducing running costs and dependence on unreliable power supplies. According to a YourStory report on the initiative, 189 women across 12 panchayats were running solar-powered irrigation enterprises. Together, they had brought irrigation to 1,410 acres, benefited more than 3,200 farmers and earned over Rs 1.28 crore.The model is also supported by the wider work of the Aga Khan Rural Support Programme in Bihar, which focuses on areas including agriculture, irrigation, renewable energy and rural livelihoods. For women like Ladli, the initiative offers more than access to technology. It provides an opportunity to manage an enterprise, earn money and become a recognised service provider in their villages.Other women are building their own livelihoodsLadli is not alone in taking this step. In nearby villages, other women have also overcome financial and social barriers to establish solar irrigation businesses. Anu Devi, from Saraffudinpur village, had to arrange money through self-help group loans, savings, family support and credit from a local shop before her pump was installed on June 14, 2023. She now provides irrigation services to around 30 farmers and has earned more than Rs 2.25 lakh. Her income helps pay for her children's education and household expenses.Sita Devi, from Mirzapur village, initially doubted whether she could manage the technology and financial responsibilities involved. After learning about the initiative from another solar entrepreneur, she decided to take the risk. Her solar irrigation system was installed in December 2023, and she has since earned more than Rs 1.5 lakh.Indu Devi’s experience reflects another side of the change. After her husband died, she became the sole breadwinner for her four children. Although some people questioned whether irrigation work was suitable for a woman, she went ahead with the business. She now supplies water to 12 farmers and has earned more than Rs 1.5 lakh. Their experiences show how access to finance, training and community support can help women take on work they may previously have considered beyond their reach.A source of income, confidence and respectFor Ladli, the significance of her solar irrigation business goes beyond the money she has earned. After a devastating loss, she has found a way to contribute to her family's financial stability while providing a useful service to fellow farmers. Her story also highlights the potential of women-led rural enterprises. When women receive access to technology, financial support and opportunities to make decisions, they can become important contributors to local economies.Solar irrigation cannot erase Ladli’s loss, but it has helped her build a new path forward. Today, as farmers turn to her for water for their fields, she is earning an income, learning new skills and gaining respect within her community. In villages where access to irrigation can determine a farmer’s ability to grow crops, Ladli’s enterprise serves a practical need. At the same time, it demonstrates how an opportunity to earn can help rural women move towards greater financial independence and a stronger voice in their own lives.You use AI every day. articles.title: A homemaker in Odisha learned to raise fish in cages inside the Hirakud Reservoir; within three years, Sujata Bhuyan was producing 25 to 30 tonnes a year and earning Rs 7 lakh to Rs 10 lakh
articles.summary: For Sujata Bhuyan, a homemaker from Odisha’s Sambalpur district, a visit to the Hirakud Reservoir opened the door to an entirely new career.
articles.body: For Sujata Bhuyan, a homemaker from Odisha’s Sambalpur district, a visit to the Hirakud Reservoir opened the door to an entirely new career. What began as a way to contribute to her family’s income gradually developed into a fish-farming business that now produces 25 to 30 metric tonnes of fish annually and earns her between Rs 7 lakh and Rs 10 lakh a year.Her journey is an example of how women can build livelihoods by learning new skills, adopting technology and making use of opportunities in their local surroundings. Bhuyan entered a field that required technical knowledge, financial investment and considerable time away from home. With training and institutional support, she gradually learned to manage the challenges and grow her enterprise. Her success also reached a national audience when Prime Minister Narendra Modi highlighted her journey in the 132nd episode of his radio programme, Mann Ki Baat, in March 2026.A visit to Hirakud sparked a business ideaBhuyan began exploring fish farming in 2022 after seeing cage-based fish cultivation in the Hirakud Reservoir. Instead of viewing the activity simply as something others were doing, she saw an opportunity to create an additional source of income for her family. She chose a method known as cage culture, in which fish are raised inside enclosed, netted structures placed in a natural water body. The cages allow water to flow through while keeping the fish within a designated space. Farmers can manage stocking, feeding and harvesting within these enclosures.The idea offered potential, but turning it into a business required more than enthusiasm. Fish farming depends on several factors, including water conditions, suitable feed, fish health and the ability to manage daily operations. Bhuyan also had to balance her new venture with household responsibilities. Weather changes and difficulties in arranging fish feed during the early stages added to the pressure. According to The New Indian Express, she approached the Fisheries Department for formal training before starting her enterprise with the help of a bank loan. Her project was estimated to cost Rs 54 lakh, and she was eligible for a 60 per cent subsidy under the Pradhan Mantri Matsya Sampada Yojana, subject to the scheme's terms.How scientific training helped her growOne of the important turning points in Bhuyan’s journey was access to technical guidance from the ICAR-Central Inland Fisheries Research Institute (ICAR-CIFRI), Barrackpore, in collaboration with the Department of Fisheries, Government of Odisha. Through training in reservoir cage culture, she learned practical aspects of fish stocking, water quality management, disease control and the operation of fish cages. This knowledge helped her understand how to manage the farm more systematically instead of relying only on trial and error.The support mattered because cage fish farming involves regular monitoring. Fish need appropriate feed and suitable water conditions to grow, while poor management can affect their health and production. Learning these practices gave Bhuyan the skills to deal with problems and make more informed decisions about her business. Her experience reflects the role that scientific institutions can play in helping people enter unfamiliar occupations. Access to training can make technical knowledge more practical for first-time entrepreneurs, particularly those who may not have previous experience in a specialised field. Within two to three years, Bhuyan had expanded her operation to produce 25 to 30 metric tonnes of fish annually. ICAR reports that her annual income reached Rs 7 lakh to Rs 10 lakh.From household income to a thriving enterpriseBuilding the fish farm required a substantial financial commitment. The reported project cost of Rs 54 lakh meant that Bhuyan had to arrange funding rather than depend on a small initial investment. According to reports, she took a bank loan of Rs 30 lakh and invested the remaining amount from her savings, while the eligible subsidy was to be provided in phases.The financial details offer an important perspective on her achievement. Fish farming at this scale is not simply a low-cost home activity. It requires investment, access to technical support and the ability to manage production and sales. Her results show what can be achieved when these elements come together, though they do not mean every new fish farmer will earn the same amount.Bhuyan’s business is also part of a wider effort to develop cage-based fisheries in the Hirakud Reservoir. Odisha has been promoting reservoir fish farming as a way to increase fish production and create opportunities for entrepreneurs. The approach has the potential to support livelihoods, but its success depends on sound farm management and responsible oversight of the reservoir environment. ICAR-CIFRI has separately worked with the Odisha Fisheries Department on environmental and aquatic animal health monitoring in the reservoir.A story of learning, confidence and opportunityWhen Prime Minister Narendra Modi mentioned Bhuyan on Mann Ki Baat, her journey became an example of how rural entrepreneurship can grow through determination and the willingness to learn. The recognition also drew attention to the possibilities within India’s fisheries sector, where scientific practices and institutional support can help people develop new livelihoods. Bhuyan’s experience challenges the idea that a homemaker’s economic contribution must remain limited to household work. She identified an opportunity, sought training, arranged financing and built the skills needed to operate a business in a technically demanding field.Her journey also offers a practical lesson for aspiring entrepreneurs: spotting an opportunity is only the beginning. Learning the process, understanding the risks, arranging funds and developing a reliable market are all essential to building a sustainable enterprise. From observing fish farming at Hirakud to producing tonnes of fish each year, Sujata Bhuyan has turned a new skill into a substantial source of income. Her story shows how the right combination of local opportunity, technical knowledge and support can help women take a more active role in their family’s finances and in the rural economy.You use AI every day. articles.title: Concern over cut to young people's mental health crisis scheme
articles.summary: The Card Before You Leave scheme ensures young people experiencing a mental health crisis who present at a hospital's emergency department are given a written appointment with specialists before leaving.
articles.body:
Concerns have been raised over the reduction of a specialist mental health support service for children and young people in the north west.

The Card Before You Leave scheme ensures young people experiencing a mental health crisis who present at a hospital's emergency department are given a written appointment with specialists before leaving.

The Western Health and Social Care Trust (WHSCT) said due to financial pressures the scheme is now only operating on a Monday to Friday basis and not at all on weekends and bank holidays.

Londonderry GP Dr Joe McEvoy said the reduction was a further "chipping away at an already threadbare service".

"It's already difficult for families when they're dealing with a young person who is distressed to know how they should manage it," McEvoy told BBC Radio Foyle's North West Today programme .

In a statement, WHSCT said the reduction was introduced in August as "part of wider savings measures" and would remain under review.

It said the reduction in the scheme's operating hours applied only to young people "who present out of hours and are assessed as low risk".

"These patients are now assessed by Child and Adolescent Mental Health Services (CAMHS) on the next working day rather than the next calendar day," the trust said.

It added: "There has been no change to arrangements for young people assessed as high risk, who continue to receive the appropriate assessment and support based on their clinical needs."

The trust said it remains "committed to providing safe and effective mental health services for children and young people".

In August, Northern Ireland's health trusts announced proposals on how they intend to make savings of up to 12% over three years.

At that time the Permanent Health Secretary, Mike Farrar, said health and social care in Northern Ireland is facing enormous challenges, with a current funding gap of £800m.

There have been no changes to the Card Before You Leave scheme in the Belfast Health Trust, Northern Trust, Southern Trust and South Eastern Trust areas.

McEvoy said weekends and bank holidays are "the times when we actually see peaks in mental health distress in young people".

The reduction, he added, means "a young person in distress on a Friday evening will now have to wait until Monday morning on a normal weekend, Tuesday morning on a bank holiday weekend and maybe a Wednesday morning on a weekend which as two-bank holidays, such as Christmas or Easter.

"It's a small change but it is a significant one," he said.

Foyle DUP MLA Julie Middleton said the decision to reduce the scheme's operating hours should be reversed.

"We should be united on calling for the service to be reinstated and we have to acknowledge that while someone could be deemed to be low risk that could move quite rapidly," she told BBC Radio Foyle.

"We need to provide a pathway where they know it's okay to ask for help, that they've asked for help and the help is coming."

SDLP MLA Mark H Durkan said the Trust's need to save money was directly "impacting on the services, not the services that people want, but the services that the population need."

He said parents should not be deterred from seeking help for their child.

"Any reduction in that service you know is going to impact people. We have to be sure the message goes out there that those deemed more at risk, even medium or high risk, that they won't be just sent home," Durkan said.

articles.title: What we know about Spain’s second high-speed rail tragedy this year
articles.summary: Officials blame a control centre order for Wednesday’s crash following a critical train signalling system failure.
articles.body:
At least 68 people were killed and about 80 injured when a high-speed train ploughed into the back of a stationary train in central Spain on Wednesday.

The crash, just before 9am (08:00 GMT) near Urda, a town south of Madrid, is Spain’s second deadly high-speed rail disaster in less than a year, and comes just weeks before national elections.

The authorities have blamed an “inexplicable” order given by a rail control centre that allowed one of the trains to resume normal speed following a signalling failure.

The moving train was run by Renfe, Spain’s state-owned rail company. It hit the rear of a stalled train operated by Iryo, a private player which entered the country’s high-speed railway service market in 2022.

Both trains were travelling from Madrid to Seville. The Renfe train was carrying 397 people and the Iryo train 147, according to the government of Castilla-La Mancha, the central region where the crash happened.

The trains collided on a raised section of track between Urda and the neighbouring town of Los Yebenes, near the ancient city of Toledo.

Two of the Iryo train’s carriages derailed and fell down the embankment during the collision, regional officials and emergency sources quoted by Spanish newspaper El Pais said.

The toll is the highest in a European rail accident since a 2013 derailment in the northwestern Spanish city of Santiago de Compostela killed 80 people.

Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez visited the site on Wednesday and declared three days of national mourning, starting on Thursday.

He pledged to get to the bottom of the crash, saying any negligence would come to light and any system failures would be met with a strong response.

At least 68 people were killed in the crash and about 80 were injured, 50 of them seriously and 15 critically, said Emiliano Garcia-Page, president of the Castilla-La Mancha regional government.

The most seriously injured people were taken to hospitals in the region and in Madrid, the capital. Others were assessed at a sports hall near the crash site, where emergency teams sorted them by the severity of their injuries before sending them home or to hospital.

Survivors treated near the scene had head wounds, facial swelling and bloodied clothing, and many were dazed, according to local media reports.

Juan Quesada, 65, who was travelling on the Renfe train to Seville for work, suffered a head injury. “A tremendous impact and so much noise, and everyone was coming at you,” he told El Pais.

A local who contributed to supplying the makeshift medical centre told the paper the scene was “like a horror movie”.

Emergency crews continue to clear the wreckage of the two trains and search for victims trapped under the rubble. Fifty-two bodies have been recovered so far.

Spain’s Civil Guard sent a disaster investigation team to the site, with evidence from the site being collected.

What caused the collision between the trains?

At about 8:30am (07:30 GMT), a computer failure knocked out LZB, the main signalling system that automatically keeps trains on the line a safe distance apart, Transport Minister Oscar Puente said.

As a result, about six trains on a 63km (39-mile) stretch stopped automatically, including the Iryo and Renfe trains. The Renfe train had been running about 25km (15.5 miles) behind the Iryo train on the same track.

Control of those trains then passed to a centre in Madrid run by Adif, the state company that manages Spain’s rail infrastructure. Its controllers had to decide when and how fast each train could move again.

At 8:36am, controllers cleared the Renfe train to resume running at its normal speed, according to the preliminary investigation by El Pais that cites train data and recordings of calls with controllers.

The Iryo train was given the same order at 8:41am but could not get moving. At 8:48am, its driver told controllers it was still stalled.

By then, the Renfe train had sped up to more than 200km/h (124mph). At 8:53am, it smashed into the stalled Iryo train.

Was human error or a signalling failure responsible?

Puente has said the crash was caused by what he called an “inexplicable” order from the control centre after the safety system failed. He said the train drivers and engineers were not to blame.

In his view, the Renfe train should never have been allowed to move while a stop signal was still showing, or should at least have been instructed to proceed slowly.

That is what Spain’s rail rules usually require. When the automatic safety system LZB goes down, trains may only move again at up to 40km/h (25mph), slow enough for the driver to spot an obstacle and stop in time.

A backup system does take over, but it detects signals only at set points along the track to determine where each train is, rather than monitoring the line continuously.

Rail engineer Jose Luis Gonzalez Vallve told the Spanish news agency EFE that the main system, which detects a train stopped ahead and can apply brakes automatically, would have prevented the crash had it been working.

According to El Pais, there was also no signal beside the track between the two trains that could have stopped the Renfe train, leaving the controllers’ instructions as the only safeguard.

The two train companies have given their own accounts. Renfe said its train moved as instructed. Sources close to Iryo told EFE its train had stopped at a signal and called controllers, as the rules require.

Adif has not yet identified the point of failure at its control centre, sources at the company told EFE.

Adif suspended high-speed train services between Madrid and the southern region of Andalusia after the crash, although trains are still running between Madrid and the nearby city of Toledo, and between the southern cities of Malaga and Seville.

Renfe has suspended ticket sales on the Madrid-Andalusia high-speed corridor until December 13, with an alternative service between Madrid and Andalusia starting from Friday.

Why has Spain suffered two deadly high-speed crashes this year?

On January 18, a high-speed train derailed near the southern town of Adamuz, in Cordoba province, and hit an oncoming train, killing 46 people. That crash also involved Renfe and Iryo trains on the same line.

Sanchez, who leads the Spanish Socialist Workers’ Party (PSOE), said the causes of the two crashes appeared unrelated, but that two high-speed rail accidents in one year were “unacceptable for a country like Spain”.

The Madrid-Seville line is Spain’s only high-speed route still using LZB, which dates from the line’s opening in 1992 and which the government is looking to update.

Adif was awarded a 52-month contract in 2021 to replace it with the European Union’s standard signalling system, but the work is still under way.

Spain has also seen two lower-speed train crashes this year, with one person killed in each and many others injured.

With elections just around the corner, the crash has taken on a political dimension in Spain.

On Wednesday evening, 1,500 people gathered in front of the Ministry of Transport in a protest organised by right-wing youth groups. They called on Puente to resign and clashed with police.

Sanchez has cancelled upcoming campaign rallies to deal with the crisis.

Alberto Nunez Feijoo, who heads the main opposition People’s Party (PP), cancelled campaign events during the mourning period and called for a full investigation.

“This is the moment to respect the dead, the injured and their families,” he said. The PP holds a slight lead over the ruling PSOE in polls.

By contrast, Santiago Abascal, leader of the far-right opposition party Vox, has not suspended campaign activities. Instead, he has adopted fiery rhetoric in response to the incident, labelling the government “a criminal organisation” and promising to take it to court.

articles.title: China deploys over 50 vessels in western Pacific, raising alarm in Taiwan, Japan & the Philippines
articles.summary: China has spread its naval forces across a vast stretch of the western Pacific, putting Taiwan, Japan and the Philippines on alert as more than 50 Chinese
articles.body: China has spread its naval forces across a vast stretch of the western Pacific, putting Taiwan, Japan and the Philippines on alert as more than 50 Chinese vessels operate across multiple strategic waters in a show of maritime reach that has raised concerns about a widening regional security threat.According to Reuters, Taiwan National Security Council secretary-general Joseph Wu warned that the simultaneous threat to the three countries was “obvious”, as he shared a map showing the scale and geographic spread of China's naval activity.Wu's map, posted on Wednesday, showed 53 Chinese vessels across the region, including 34 navy warships and the aircraft carrier Liaoning.“We're staying vigilant about their activities,” Wu said, warning that the deployments raised concerns beyond Taiwan's immediate surroundings.The vessels were spread across several strategically important waters, with the Liaoning and its accompanying battle group positioned east of the Philippines, other Chinese naval formations operating off Taiwan's eastern and southeastern coasts, and three formations located off southern Japan.China's defence ministry said the Liaoning aircraft carrier group sailed into the western Pacific on October 14 for training under the Chinese navy's annual routine exercise plan.The navy said the drills were intended to test and improve the group's combat readiness and mission capabilities, adding that they complied with international law and were “not directed at any specific country or target”.The deployment places Chinese naval forces across a broad stretch of the western Pacific, potentially increasing the surveillance and defence demands on Taiwan and its regional partners.Japan's defence ministry separately said it had tracked three Chinese warships and a Chinese Coast Guard vessel passing through the Osumi Strait, off the southwestern island of Kyushu, on Tuesday before entering the Pacific Ocean.
