articles.title: Russell Brand's wife tells his rape trial he is 'kind and a wonderful father'
articles.summary: Laura Brand tells the jury at his trial she feels "very seen by him" and "I love him very much".
articles.body:
Warning: This story contains graphic content.

Russell Brand's wife Laura has told a court her husband is "caring, kind and a wonderful father to our children".

The 39-year-old told the jury at his rape and sexual assault trial that "the way he treats me is to know me", adding: "I feel very seen by him... I love him very much."

The media personality faces seven charges - three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one of attempted indecent assault. He denies all the charges and has pleaded not guilty.

Giving evidence at Southwark Crown Court in London on Thursday, Laura Brand was asked by the defence barrister if her husband respected her when she didn't want to be sexual with him, and she replied: "Yes absolutely."

Laura Brand is the daughter of former golfer Bernard Gallacher and sister of TV presenter Kirsty Gallacher. She married Brand in 2017 and they have three children.

She told the court she first met him at the Edinburgh festival in 2006, explaining that he took her number and they started a relationship soon afterwards.

She said that after his performance: "I went over and said, 'I'm Laura, Kirsty's sister. That was a great show'."

He contacted her the next day, she said. When they met, she said they had oral sex, adding: "He might have wanted to have sex but I didn't want to."

Laura Brand said she knew before they met that "he liked women", and found out that while they were dating that he had been involved with others.

"I wasn't interested in having a relationship with him if he was sleeping with other people", she said.

"I was invested, we both had told each other we loved each other, but it was clear it was difficult for him to be monogamous."

She said she remained friends with Brand while he was married to singer Katy Perry from 2010 to 2012, and got back together with him in 2015.

Asked if she was "aware of his promiscuity" during their time apart, she said: "I was very aware of it. I could read about it regularly in the papers, so I was aware of it and he also told me."

Turning to their relationship now, she said: "We have a very honest, frank, and clear relationship and marriage.

"It is one of the most important parts of our marriage, and our relationship has always been honest."

The charges against Brand relate to allegations made by six female complainants spanning a 10-year period between 1999 and 2009.

The entertainer has displayed little emotion during the course of his trial, but was seen smiling broadly during parts of his wife's evidence.

He let out a laugh when she told the court: "We do have many friends and there are colleagues, and we are grateful for those people."

Her evidence came a day after the star appeared in the witness box himself.

He told the jury the allegations had a "devastating" impact on his relationships with friends and colleagues, meaning they would not touch him "with a bargepole".

He also said on Wednesday he had been promiscuous but believes sexual consent is "fundamental, essential, necessary and indeed in many ways more important than sex itself".

On Thursday, the court also heard statements from two of Russell Brand's ex-girlfriends

Elia Alvarez Diaz said they were in a relationship and lived together for about a year from 1998 to 1999, and described the defendant as "gentle" and "loving".

She described him as being "highly persuasive... a complex character" and "exciting to be with".

"When I said no, however, he accepted it," she said in a statement.

Their relationship ended because he cheated on her repeatedly, she said.

Amanda Alguero Alejos told the court in a statement that Brand had also repeatedly cheated on her.

"He was undoubtedly promiscuous, never in front of me and never when I was around. That was not what mattered to me at the time," she said.

She recalled women "circling" around Brand "like birds", even when they were out as a couple.

The trial continues, with the jury likely to retire to consider the verdicts on Tuesday.

articles.title: Pentagon says Iran war has cost US taxpayers $47bn: What that means
articles.summary: With five days to go before the US midterms, analysts say the war could affect how people vote.
articles.body:
The Pentagon has told lawmakers in the United States that the war on Iran has cost American taxpayers at least $47.1bn so far.

The estimate, disclosed last week, comes just days before the November 3 midterm elections, which will determine if US President Donald Trump’s Republican Party will maintain control of Congress for the next two years.

In a statement on Wednesday the Pentagon also said it had “successfully obligated 97.5 percent” of the funds Trump provided the department. Last July, Trump signed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBA) outlining tax and spending plans, which came into effect earlier this year.

We take a close look at the Pentagon estimate, and what it means for the US economy and the midterm elections.

What has the Pentagon spending report revealed?

The Pentagon told Congress that the cost of the US-Israel war on Iran as of October 16 had risen to at least $47.1bn.

Congress officials shared the Pentagon’s cost estimate breakdown with The New York Times.

According to the Times and other US media reports, the Pentagon’s estimate covers the operational costs of the war and includes a projected cost of $29bn needed to replace expended munitions such as bombs, bullets and other military hardware that has been deployed in the war so far.

It also reveals that since the war started on February 28, the US Air Force has spent $7.6bn on fighter and bomber units; the US Navy has spent $1.5bn on two dozen warships and aircraft carriers; and the US Army has spent $2.1bn to sustain its troops in the Middle East.

According to the US Central Command, there are more than 50,000 American troops stationed in the Middle East, comprising personnel deployed to large, permanent bases and to smaller forward sites across the region.

Officials told the Times that the Pentagon has spent $6.1bn to replace damaged aircraft and munitions, $645m on transport and support for commandos in the region and $24.5m on “in-house medical support” for US service members.

A congressional official added that the US Transportation Command also spent $92.2m to move equipment, and the US Cyber Command spent $14m on “cyber support operations”.

The Pentagon’s estimate, however, does not include how much Washington will need to spend to repair its damaged military bases across the Middle East and also does not take into account the cost of fuel, which is needed to power ships and aircraft used in the war.

While the Pentagon has publicly acknowledged 18 US service member fatalities in the war, The Washington Post has cited six unnamed US officials stating the true death toll is at least 22. According to the official Pentagon Defense Casualty Analysis System (DCAS) database, 865 military personnel have been wounded in the war with Iran.

According to an October 19 report by USA Today, five senators from the Democratic Party had written to Admiral Brad Cooper, the head of US Central Command, demanding that the Pentagon reveal the true cost of the war. Their letter said the Trump administration’s “ongoing efforts to hide the true cost of this war are outrageous and unacceptable”.

Trump has not commented on the latest Pentagon estimate. But the Trump administration’s war on Iran has grown increasingly unpopular with US citizens due to its impact on US and global energy costs.

Since early March, shortly after the war began, Iran has closed the critical Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf, through which about one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas supplies were shipped until then. This has sent the price of oil spiralling and caused shortages globally. In the US, diesel, which is heavily relied on by farmers and small businesses, has nearly doubled in price.

In a post on X following the latest Pentagon report, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York wrote: “For eight months, American families have been buried by the heavy cost of Trump’s disastrous war in Iran.

“Trump and his ego led us into this war with no plan, no authority, and no exit strategy,” he added.

How does the Pentagon’s estimate compare with past calculations?

Estimates for the cost of the Iran war to the US have risen steadily as the war has continued.

The Pentagon’s latest estimate is higher than the $38bn the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) forecast in September.

It is also higher than the $37.5bn price tag that US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth gave in July this year. Hegseth confirmed this amount during a hearing before the Senate appropriations committee and added that the cost covered some operations and maintenance extending through to the end of September.

Hegseth’s July estimate was already about $8bn higher than the previous figure released by the administration of President Donald Trump in May – $29bn.

Prior to the May estimate, in late April the Pentagon’s comptroller Jules Hurst reported that the war would cost $25bn.

Meanwhile, with the war entering its ninth month and no peace deal in sight, last month the CBO said the war with Iran could cost approximately $2bn to $3bn per month for as long as it continues.

The Pentagon’s inspector general also said last month that US troops are facing “strategic inventory shortfalls” as the war continues.

But the Trump administration has denied it is running low on weapons stockpiles.

“Cowards and traitors would like to say that the United States is short of ammunition, but that is not true. We have more ammunition than we could ever imagine using. And we are producing it at levels we have never reached before,” Trump told the United Nations General Assembly in New York in September.

Trump has also repeatedly stated that the Iran war will end when he wants it to.

Last week at an election rally in Texas, according to a report by CNBC, Trump said: “Somebody asked me before, ‘When will the war in Iran end?’ I said, ‘Whenever I want it to end.’”

What does the rising cost of the war mean for the midterm elections?

The US-Israel war on Iran has affected the US economy through direct government spending as well as rising energy and fuel costs.

On Wednesday, the average price of a gallon of diesel in the US hit $6.35, compared with $3.75 last year, according to the American Automobile Association.

Higher fuel costs are also driving up the cost of food – with shortages of oil and gas affecting nearly every stage of the food supply chain.

Meanwhile, the country’s national debt has surpassed a record $40 trillion, two years before expected.

As a result, the war has become deeply unpopular in the US and Trump’s approval ratings have slumped to just 33 percent – the lowest they have been at any time during his two terms as president.

With five days to go before the midterms, analysts say confirmation by the Pentagon of the high cost of the war is likely to affect how people in the US vote.

Currently, the Democrats lead Republicans by 51.4 percent to 43.2 percent, a gap of 8.2 percentage points, according to RealClearPolling’s national polling average.

Chris Featherstone, a political scientist from the University of York in the United Kingdom, said this is an issue that hits at two key pillars of Trump’s political rhetoric: his promise to initiate “no new wars” during his campaign for the presidency in 2024, and his emphasis on fixing the American economy.

“The spiralling cost of the conflict for the taxpayer, and the lack of a clear end point resembles the critiques Trump levelled at the war in Afghanistan in his first presidential election campaign,” he told Al Jazeera.

According to the Costs of War Project at Brown University, the war in Afghanistan, which began in 2001, cost the US an estimated $2.26 trillion to $2.3 trillion in total across multiple presidential administrations, including George W Bush, Barack Obama and Donald Trump.

“While many of Trump’s most loyal MAGA voters are likely to remain loyal to Trump in the midterms despite the cost of the Iran conflict, the more peripheral supporters seem to be drifting away from the president ahead of the midterms, and the significant impact of this conflict on cost of living appears to be a major factor,” Featherstone said.

articles.title: ‘Survival of the fittest’: The struggle to get to university in The Gambia
articles.summary: Students at a top university protest against transport shortages, poor facilities and safety concerns.
articles.body:
Faraba Banta, The Gambia – For Muhammed Lamin Jallow, a student at the University of The Gambia’s School of Arts and Sciences, getting to class has become a daily struggle.

He travels about 40 km (25 miles) from home to the Faraba Banta campus, depending on university buses, to attend lectures.

But securing a seat on the bus can be challenging.

“Sometimes, it feels like survival of the fittest,” he told Al Jazeera. “We compete as to who gets in first, who gets to sit, who gets to stand and who goes to school and who does not.”

Jallow was among hundreds of students who protested at the University of The Gambia (UTG) on Monday, taking their grievances over transportation, campus facilities and student welfare to the vice chancellor’s office.

Lectures have since resumed after the government promised improvements to campus services.

But the students have more demands. They want Vice Chancellor Herbert Robinson and the director of student affairs to resign, accusing both officials of failing to perform their duties.

While the government has announced measures to address some of the concerns, the leadership dispute remains unresolved.

Transport and basic services remain concerns

The Students’ Union says its concerns affect more than 12,000 students, many of whom depend on university buses to reach campus.

Following the protest, Higher Education Minister Professor Pierre Gomez visited the campus with university representatives and officials from the Ministry of Communications and Digital Economy.

In a statement, the Ministry of Higher Education, Research, Science and Technology said the Gambia Transport Service Company had deployed 20 buses to support student transportation.

Students have also complained of limited access to safe drinking water and affordable food, as well as unreliable internet connectivity.

In response, the ministry promised that cafeterias across the university were ready to serve students and staff, but acknowledged that additional filtration was needed to make campus water safe for drinking. Water jars and dispensers have been installed at designated points, and the National Water and Electricity Company (NAWEC) had been consulted, it said.

On internet access, the ministry said work was under way to extend connectivity to the newly constructed Schools of Agriculture and Law, with completion expected within a week.

The proposals are intended to support student access to research materials and other educational resources. However, the statement did not confirm whether the work had been completed.

The ministry said it would continue working with the university, the students’ union and other relevant stakeholders to monitor implementation.

Cafeterias and practical training facilities

The reopening of cafeterias was another demand raised by students, who had complained that their closure made it difficult to find affordable meals on campus.

Ismaila Fadera, the students’ union president, said he raised the issue with Robinson on October 20 .

Fadera quoted the vice chancellor as saying: “Mister president, I have the student interest at heart, but we must balance this against administrative processes and compliance. You know I was a student too and many of us went through that. I used to carry my own water and food in my bag to university. The students should be told the reality. Having a cafeteria is a great addition to enhance the student experience but it is not right.”

The ministry said the cafeterias were ready to serve students and staff, although it provided no details on meal prices or availability at individual facilities.

Beyond food and water, students say inadequate learning facilities are affecting their education, particularly in programmes that require practical training.

At the School of Medicine and Allied Health Sciences in Banjul, students face overcrowded classrooms, inadequate ventilation, malfunctioning electrical sockets and shortages of projectors and smartboards, according to Abubacarr Manneh, president of the University of The Gambia Medical Students Association. Manneh said medical, nursing and postgraduate nursing students share the available facilities, putting pressure on classroom space.

He also worries about shortages of practical training equipment, including a promised simulation laboratory where students could develop clinical skills.

“Practical sessions are crucial in our professional training and development for better care of our patients,” he told Al Jazeera.

The university’s journalism students have similar concerns

Sukai Fatajo, a journalism student who participated in the protest, said the school needed radio and television studios to help students develop practical skills.

“We deserve better, and our demands must be met,” she told Al Jazeera.

The students’ union has also called for functional science laboratories, improvements to facilities at the medical school and adequate staffing.

For Kumba Leigh, a journalism student, the struggle to reach the university has also become a question of personal safety.

One morning in April, Leigh was attacked by a knife-wielding assailant in her hometown of Bakau as she walked to a bus stop. She was trying to leave home early enough to secure a seat.

The attacker threatened to kill her if she did not hand over her bag. When she resisted, he struck her on the head and shoulder, cut her bag and dislocated her right arm. A nearby shopkeeper intervened, forcing the assailant to flee.

Months later, Leigh still has pain in her arm and suffers from trauma.

“No one should have to risk their life simply to travel to school,” she told Al Jazeera, calling for stronger security and increased police patrols.

articles.title: Israel’s election rhetoric: What candidates said, and how they performed
articles.summary: From Netanyahu to Ben-Gvir, campaign boasts and attacks on Arab parties have been met with a deadlocked result.
articles.body:
Israel’s parliamentary election on Tuesday produced no clear winner, with nearly 90 percent of ballots counted and both major political blocs falling short of the 61 seats needed to form a government.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc is on course to win 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset, while the opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot is expected to secure 48 seats.

The Arab-majority parties won 19 seats, a historic high, driven by record turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel of about 80 percent. That has placed the Arab parties at the centre of coalition arithmetic, even as several party leaders ruled out governing with them.

So what did the main contenders say in the run-up to and during the vote, and how did they fare? Here is a look:

Benjamin Netanyahu, Likud: Elections ‘stolen by Arab parties’

Pre-election: In the build-up to the election, Netanyahu expressed confidence, telling The Jerusalem Post on October 22, “I’m gonna have five more terms.”

On Sunday, he targeted the opposition, with Haaretz citing a broadcast on Israel’s Channel 14 that Netanyahu warned if they win, they will “give citizenship to hundreds of thousands of Palestinians”, a move that would signal the “end of the Jewish state”.

Election day: On Tuesday, he said forming a government with Arab-led parties would be “a shame and a disgrace”.

“It is forbidden – simply forbidden – to endanger Israel and to establish a government that relies on anti-Zionist Arab parties,” he told supporters.

Post-election day: After the elections, Netanyahu’s Likud party took aim at Palestinian citizens of Israel who voted.

In a party statement shared by Netanyahu, it claimed the elections “were stolen by Arab parties that support terrorism and the elimination of the Jewish state through serious criminal offences”. According to The Times of Israel, police and the Central Elections Committee have already dismissed these claims.

What the results show: Likud is on course for 26 seats, the largest party, with 20.65 percent of the vote. But his bloc has 53 seats, eight short of a majority.

Gadi Eisenkot, Yashar Party: ‘I do not see an Arab party that accepts my principles’

Pre-election: In a September interview with The Jerusalem Post, he dismissed the idea he would need to form a coalition with Arab parties: “I believe the majority we receive will be much larger than what the polls currently show,” adding “I do not see an Arab party that accepts my principles.”

He also said his “inner feeling is that I now have the ability to defeat Netanyahu”.

Election day: Eisenkot rallied Israelis to get rid of “the worst government Israel has known”.

However, he acknowledged how tight the race was, saying, “We are on perhaps the most critical day since the founding of the state.”

Post-election day: On Wednesday, Eisenkot told his supporters the Israeli public “voted against” Netanyahu and promised, “to ensure that the people’s decision is translated into a Zionist government”.

What the results show: Yashar is on course for 21 seats, with 16.16 percent. His bloc has 48, 13 short of a majority, and he cannot reach 61 without the Arab-led parties.

Naftali Bennett, Together Party: ‘The October 7 government is going home’

Pre-election: In February, months before the vote, Bennett told a closed conference of party activists that he stood by his 2021 decision to govern with Ra’am, but said he would not repeat it.

He said, “We will establish a unity government under my leadership … We are going to win, and we are going to form it,” Israel National News reported.

Election day: “Netanyahu has lost, and the October 7 government is going home,” Bennett told supporters in Tel Aviv.

Post-election: In a post on X, Bennett told Israelis to “lift your heads” and said he will do everything “to establish a Zionist Alliance of Servants government”.

What the results show: Together is on course for 12 seats with 9.07 percent, narrowly behind the Joint List.

Itamar Ben-Gvir, Otzma Yehudit: Palestinians in Gaza ‘shouldn’t live’

Pre-election: In his election campaign, Ben-Gvir expressed his most genocidal views yet, saying in August that there are Palestinians in Gaza “who are not worthy of life. They shouldn’t live. They’re not even people.” He called for Israel to kill “30 to 40” people in Gaza every night.

Election day: “If you want this country to stay Jewish and Zionist, if you don’t want it to be in the hands of (Israeli Knesset members) Mansour Abbas and Ahmad Tibi, go out and vote,” he told supporters at the entrance to the Arab city of Kafr Qasim.

What the results show: Otzma Yehudit is on course for seven seats, with 5.58 percent, less than half of the 15 he wanted.

Bezalel Smotrich, Religious Zionism-Zehut: ‘Jewish settlements will be established in Gaza’

Pre-election: In a statement he issued in August, he promised an expansion of his settlement “revolution” with a programme for the “Judaization of the Negev and the Galilee” at the expense of Palestinians, as part of his campaign.

Election day: He warned on Facebook of high turnout in communities of Palestinian citizens of Israel, claiming that failing to mobilise right-wing voters could let “terror supporters” into government.

That night, he told supporters “Jewish settlements will be established in Gaza.”

What the results show: Religious Zionism is on course for six seats, with 4.78 percent.

Yousef Jabareen, Joint List: ‘Change comes through Jewish-Arab partnership, a true and equal partnership’

Pre-election: In August, he stated that only “a large and strong Joint List will work with all its might to send the Netanyahu/Ben-Gvir/Smotrich government home”, according to The Jerusalem Post.

Election day, night: In a video statement, he said Netanyahu knew “we can put an end to his bloody reign.”

Post-election: He wrote on X that his party was ready for the “ousting of the Netanyahu government”, which he called one of “bloodshed”.

“Against a politics of supremacy, racism, and exclusion, we offer a completely different alternative. The change comes through Jewish-Arab partnership, a true and equal partnership,” he wrote.

What the results show: The Joint List is on course for 12 seats with 9.14 percent, making it the third-largest party by vote share.

Mansour Abbas, Ra’am: Netanyahu uses ‘scare tactic to mobilise right-wing voters’

Election day, night: In July, Abbas set Ra’am a goal of at least seven seats, enough, he argued, to make it the balance of power in a “government of change”.

Election day: He hit back at Netanyahu’s posts about Palestinian citizens of Israel, stating in a video that he was “lying and inciting against Ra’am, using it as a scare tactic to mobilise right-wing voters and drive them to the polls”.

What the results show: Ra’am is on course for eight seats, with 6.09 percent, beating his target of seven.

Avigdor Lieberman, Yisrael Beiteinu: ‘We will reach 61 seats’

Pre-election: On October 15, he claimed: “We will reach 61 seats or more for the change bloc.”

Election day: He urged patience, saying on Friday, “we’ll be able to talk about a much better and more optimistic picture.”

What the results show: Yisrael Beiteinu is on course for seven seats, with 5.93 percent.

Yair Lapid, Together: Netanyahu is ‘busy fear-mongering’

Pre-election: In September, he posted a statement which said, “Netanyahu ignored every warning before October 7, and now, 28 days before the election, he’s suddenly busy fear-mongering.”

Election day: He declared victory, stating, “The Netanyahu bloc has suffered a crushing defeat.”

What the results show: Together, which he co-leads with Bennett, is on course for 12 seats, with 9.07 percent.

articles.title: What we know of Vance’s letter to Rezaei, as Trump warns Gulf to ‘prepare’
articles.summary: Letter to Iran’s security chief reportedly pushes for swift return to peace talks, with Vance leading US delegation.
articles.body:
United States Vice President JD Vance has sent a letter to Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, in an 11th-hour push to restart peace talks, according to US media reports.

The letter, which has reportedly been “received well” by Iran, aimed to gauge whether the US and Iran can narrow their differences enough to stave off a potential new round of US strikes on Iran, The Wall Street Journal has reported.

The outreach comes as Trump warns the US’s Gulf allies to prepare themselves for a brief, high-intensity military campaign after next week’s US midterm elections , according to the Journal. Trump previously said the US may “do another little Epic Fury”, referring to the military operation against Iran that began in February.

So, what does Vance’s letter mean for the prospects of renewed US-Iran conflict – or a return to negotiations?

Vance’s letter to Rezaei, who heads Iran’s Supreme National Security Council , has not been published, but several US media outlets have reported on its contents.

The Journal quoted an informed source as saying the letter and follow-up discussions did not cover specific peace terms, but rather a potential “framework for negotiations”.

Another source told the Journal the goal was to see if “Tehran and Washington could find enough common ground to persuade Trump not to give a final order for a short, intense attack on Iran in the coming weeks”.

The New York Times reported that Vance’s letter proposed a meeting between US and Iranian officials soon, with Vance heading a US delegation as he did during previous US-Iran talks in June .

The Times reported the letter was passed to Rezaei by Qatari mediators on Sunday. Vance called for direct talks and said Iran’s nuclear programme would have to be on the table from the outset, according to US and Iranian officials quoted by the media.

If Iran accepts, the negotiations could take place as soon as next week, said the officials, naming Qatar or Turkiye as possible venues.

Iran has not publicly commented on the letter, but the Times reported that it had been “received well by Iran’s leaders”.

Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi also spoke of ongoing negotiations in a social media post on Wednesday, saying Iran “continues to give diplomacy a chance”.

Rezaei is expected to officially respond to Vance’s letter on Thursday, according to the Times.

Hamidreza Azizi, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group, told Al Jazeera that Vance’s move to address the letter to Rezaei is significant, reflecting a possible shift in Washington’s view of who holds influence in Tehran.

“This could indicate that the Americans believe changes in Tehran’s internal power dynamics have created better prospects for achieving something through direct engagement with Rezaei,” he said.

How is this letter different from previous US attempts at talks?

Vance has consistently appeared more averse to drawn-out military conflict with Iran than Trump. While publicly backing the war, the vice president reportedly preferred to continue with more intensive diplomacy before the US joined Israel in the war on Iran in February. He has since privately voiced concerns about the protracted conflict, according to US media reports.

There have been mixed messages, however, regarding Trump’s input in Vance’s latest outreach attempt. The Journal reported that Trump directed Vance to send the letter to Rezaei, but Trump later disputed that.

Speaking to reporters, Trump said he had given Vance the go-ahead to reach out to Iran, but characterised the initiative as aimed at helping Iran “with medical supplies and various things”.

Ali Vaez, deputy programme director for the Middle East and North Africa at the International Crisis Group, told Al Jazeera that Tehran sees Vance as “someone who has both the president’s ear and an appreciation of the price of failure”.

“Unlike Trump, who sees escalation as a source of leverage, Vance appears more attuned to its diminishing returns,” said Vaez. “But a more credible messenger alone cannot bridge a chasm of substantive disagreements.”

Rouzbeh Parsi, an Iran analyst who is an affiliated researcher at Lund University’s Department of History and Human Rights Studies in Sweden, described Vance as the “voice of reason” on Iran within the Trump administration, saying his signals have been “the least volatile and unpredictable”.

However, Parsi told Al Jazeera that Vance’s position has “never proven to be sturdy enough to actually sway Trump”.

“Thus, while the optics with Vance look better than anyone else in the Trump administration, I doubt that they [Iranian officials] give the outreach much credence until Vance proves able to actually deliver something on his own,” he said.

Azizi also said Tehran is aware of the limits of Vance’s influence within Trump’s administration.

“We have seen two wars in less than a year, despite Vance’s objections and differing views,” he said. “For that reason, I believe the leadership in Tehran still views US initiatives and military threats with considerable suspicion.

“At the end of the day, Trump makes the final decisions – and that he has proven to be unpredictable and difficult to trust – remains a major factor shaping Iranian decision-making at this moment,” Azizi added.

Why has Trump warned Gulf states to ‘prepare’?

Trump has reportedly told Gulf allies to prepare for renewed conflict amid signs they could be increasingly exposed to Iranian retaliation.

Tehran has repeatedly warned that it will respond more aggressively to any new wave of US-Israeli attacks, including by hitting oil sites, undersea cables, data centres and AI facilities in the Gulf.

“Our strategy is ‘zero red lines’,” said Mehdi Mohammadi, an adviser to Iran’s Parliament Speaker Mohammad Ghalibaf in a statement on October 21.

Against that backdrop, Gulf countries have stepped up diplomacy with Iran, with Saudi and Qatari diplomats, along with officials from Pakistan and Turkiye, participating in talks with Iranian officials in Tehran on Monday.

Is a US strike likely after the midterms next week?

Vaez said the risk is “dangerously high”, with the November 3 elections possibly marking “the expiration of [Trump’s] political restraint.”

“The military machinery is being assembled and the diplomatic clock is running down,” said Vaez. “It’s a mistake to think Trump will be a lame duck after the midterms. He’s more likely to become a flame duck, taking bigger risks.”

Marzieh Kouhi Esfahani, assistant professor of politics and international relations of the Middle East at Durham University, UK, also said the likelihood of new strikes is “quite high”.

“Both sides are determined to get out of this no-war-no-peace stalemate,” she told Al Jazeera. “The likelihood of that… moving towards more war is much higher than peace.”

Parsi said a potential new military campaign could be extremely destructive.

“Since both sides feel the pressure to prove themselves, this coming military exchange will be more significant and cause more devastation and bloodshed,” he said.

articles.title: Popular airline hits customers with steep fee hike for first time in 8 years
articles.summary: American Airlines' Citi AAdvantage Platinum Select and Business MasterCard annual fees jump from $99 to $150, but new perks may offset the cost. An expert weighs in.
articles.body: The era of the standard $99 airline credit card may be fading as American Airlines becomes the latest major carrier to adjust its price tag. Beginning Jan. 24, 2027, the annual fee for both the Citi/AAdvantage Platinum Select MasterCard and the Citi/AAdvantage Business MasterCard will jump from $99 to $150, according to a company press release. The adjustment marks the first price hike for the popular Platinum Select consumer card since 2018, signaling a shift in the travel rewards landscape. MAJOR AIRLINE DITCHES SNACKS DURING SHORT FLIGHTS AS ‘ZERO SERVICE’ SPARKS DEBATE To soften the blow of a nearly 52% fee increase, American Airlines, Citi and MasterCard are adding several new travel and lifestyle perks. Whether those additions make up for the $51 increase will depend largely on how travelers use the card, Nick Ewen, editor-in-chief of The Points Guy, told Fox News Digital. "You have to look at the real dollar value based on your own travel habits," said Ewen, who is based in Florida. Cardholders will gain additional ways to earn AAdvantage miles on everyday spending, along with up to $120 toward Global Entry or TSA PreCheck application fees every four years, American Airlines confirmed. Additionally, a new $100 annual statement credit for in-flight purchases will replace the previous 25% food and beverage discount. This makes the card significantly more rewarding for travelers, as the credit can be applied toward broad in-flight expenses, including Wi-Fi, which was explicitly excluded under the old discount system. "You may not be able to stomach that additional increased annual fee." For someone who regularly spends money aboard American flights or already pays for Global Entry or TSA PreCheck, Ewen said the new credits could help offset the higher annual fee. "If the answer is yes, you're definitely going to come out ahead," he said of travelers who typically spend up to $100 on in-flight purchases each year. PASSENGER JET BOUND FOR US PLUNGES 27,000 FEET BEFORE CIRCLING FOR HOURS The changes may not be for everyone, however. "If you're only flying American once a year, you may not be able to stomach that additional increased annual fee," he said. The changes also include adjustments to how cardholders can rack up rewards on everyday purchases, according to the press release. The personal Platinum Select card will offer three miles per dollar on eligible AAdvantage Hotels and Cars bookings and two miles per dollar on gas and EV charging, select streaming services, and eligible Rides and Rails purchases. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Existing perks — including preferred boarding, no foreign transaction fees and a free first checked bag on domestic American itineraries for the cardholder and up to four companions — will remain intact. Ewen said the higher fee follows a broader shift among airline rewards cards. "American is far from the first airline that we've seen this increase in their annual fees," he said, pointing to similar changes from Delta, Southwest and United. Entry-level airline cards that once hovered around $100 annually are increasingly moving closer to $150, Ewen said. "This is definitely the norm, although it's not universal across the board," he added. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES The move by American Airlines aligns with a broader trend sweeping the credit card sector. Over the past few years, the travel rewards market has seen steady fee inflation as issuers pack mid-tier and premium cards with statement credits and subscription services. The move by American Airlines aligns with a broader trend sweeping the credit card sector. Financial institutions are betting consumers will accept higher upfront costs in exchange for tangible, use-it-or-lose-it perks, transforming traditional flight-focused credit cards into broader lifestyle products, according to reports. The changes drew mixed reactions from cardholders online. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "Call me crazy, but none of this is an upgrade," one Reddit user commented. Another questioned the value of the new in-flight credit. "These inflight credit[s] [are] annoying," the person wrote. "They don't even stock them except for longer flights." Others were more receptive to the new benefits, with one commenter pointing to the Global Entry or TSA PreCheck credit as a reason the higher fee could be worthwhile. articles.title: Victims appalled as deadly crush footage included in Call of Duty
articles.summary: Modern Warfare 4 uses video from the Itaewon crush to show the aftermath of an imagined North Korean attack.
articles.body:
Families who lost loved ones in a crush caused by overcrowding in Seoul's narrow streets four years ago say they're appalled to see footage of it on the latest Call of Duty game.

In an opening scene of Modern Warfare 4, video of rescue efforts from the 2022 disaster in Itaewon, South Korea, is used to show the aftermath of an imagined attack from North Korea.

Almost 160 people died and their families are calling on the game's makers Activision to delete the footage, saying including it was "senseless".

Activision confirmed it used recordings from that night but had "not intended to reference or trivialise the Itaewon disaster or any other real-world tragedy in any way, shape or form".

"In developing Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, we approached the subject matter with care and respect," a spokesperson said.

"The game's opening cinematic utilises some real world news coverage to establish the game's fictional narrative."

Thursday marks the fourth anniversary of the crush, which happened when more than 100,000 people went out in Seoul's nightlife district to celebrate Halloween.

The narrow streets became so tightly packed that people could not move and some were unable to breathe.

"We cannot help but be appalled that the chaotic and desperate scene, in which many citizens at the site performed CPR to save one another and victims lay on the freezing street, was used as it was to create a scene in a game," the bereaved families said.

"Using such an event as material for a game made for entertainment is in itself highly inappropriate and senseless," their statement continued.

"If the game developer has even a minimum of courtesy and empathy towards the victims, it should take corrective action without delay."

Activision did not comment on the request to edit the scene to remove the video from that night.

Modern Warfare 4, which was released last week, had already faced criticism for basing the game on North Korea invading South Korea, as the two countries have been technically at war for decades.

Fighting stopped in Korean War in 1953, but the two countries never signed a peace treaty and conflict is a very real worry in that part of the world.

At the launch of the game, Call of Duty's chief marketing officer, Tyler Bahl, told Newsbeat: "We have to understand this is entertainment".

articles.title: Minnesota prosecutors have charged conservative activists James O'Keefe and Cam Higby with two felonies after an undercover voting stunt, though both say they were testing election rules and neither cast a ballot
articles.summary: Two conservative activists in Minnesota are facing felony charges after an undercover exercise at polling stations during the August 11 primary election.
articles.body: Two conservative activists in Minnesota are facing felony charges after an undercover exercise at polling stations during the August 11 primary election. James O'Keefe and Cam Higby visited several polling stations and used the names of registered voters while asking for ballots. They filmed the exercise to test the state's election rules and later shared the videos online. Although neither man actually voted, Hennepin County prosecutors charged them with unlawful voting and identity theft on Wednesday.O'Keefe and Higby maintain that they were conducting an investigation, not trying to cast illegal votes. Prosecutors, however, say their actions went beyond testing the rules because they used other people's identities without permission.According to the Hennepin County Attorney's Office, the two men gave election workers names belonging to voters registered at the polling stations they visited. Some of those names belonged to people who had died, while at least one belonged to someone who had already voted, MPR News reported.Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty said the absence of an actual vote did not change the allegations. "I think it’s pretty clear they did not intend to vote. That’s not the question here," she told reporters on Wednesday, as quoted by MPR news.What were the two activists trying to prove?The videos show the activists visiting polling stations in Minneapolis to examine how election workers check voters' identities and handle people seeking to register on Election Day.In one recording, Higby explained that they wanted to find out whether people could vote without showing identification. They also planned to see whether someone could help another person register without being registered to vote themselves.The exercise focused particularly on Minnesota's 'vouching system', which allows a registered voter to confirm the address of someone who wants to register on Election Day.O'Keefe was filmed asking election workers about this procedure while speaking in an accent. The workers explained how the system operated, and his team subsequently left the polling station. Videos also showed members of the group wearing burqas outside polling stations.The activists later presented the recordings as part of their investigation into possible weaknesses in Minnesota's voting system. But state officials disputed the suggestion that the videos showed election workers failing to follow the rules.Minnesota Secretary of State Steve Simon said the workers had acted correctly and followed the required election procedures.How Minnesota allows people to register?Unlike systems where voters must complete registration before election day, Minnesota offers several ways for eligible people to register when they arrive at a polling station.One option is vouching. A person who is already registered in the same voting precinct can accompany an unregistered voter and confirm where that person lives.The registered voter must sign an oath confirming the address. Minnesota law allows one registered voter to vouch for up to eight people.O'Keefe and Higby were examining this arrangement because they wanted to see how election workers would respond when someone sought to use it.However, prosecutors say the law also makes it illegal to deliberately give a false identity while applying for a ballot. They argue that this restriction applies even when the person does not go on to vote.Neither activist signed the oath required for vouching. Moriarty said signing it falsely could have resulted in a separate felony perjury allegation. Instead, the present charges concern the identities the men allegedly used while requesting ballots.What O'Keefe and Higby sayO'Keefe's group, which describes itself as the "Justice League", defended the exercise in a statement issued in August. It said the participants "did not cast ballots. The investigation was intended to test the limits of Minnesota’s vouching law and document how election workers apply it on Election Day."Higby also rejected the allegations after prosecutors announced the charges. In a social media post seeking financial support, he accused Minnesota officials of trying to imprison him "for exposing election vulnerabilities in their state."O'Keefe is known for producing undercover recordings. His previous activities have also led to criminal charges. In 2017, Washington Post reporters uncovered an attempt by O'Keefe to persuade the newspaper to publish a false story.What happens next in the case?The Minnesota Secretary of State's Office had alerted prosecutors to the activists' activities during the primary election. Following an investigation, both men were charged with unlawful voting and identity theft.According to MPR News, court records show that the particular election-related charges involved in this case have been used only once in Minnesota since 2021.Moriarty said the case was not about whether the activists' behaviour was offensive or intended to attract attention. The concern, she explained, was their alleged use of other voters' identities inside polling stations. "It is not against the law to be performative. It is not against the law to be offensive," she said.Simon also supported the action against the two men, saying election workers should be able to carry out their duties without being deceived or disrupted.Both O'Keefe and Higby are scheduled to appear in court on November 16.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A week of Israel’s lockdown in Hebron: What’s happened, when will it end?
articles.summary: Israel is imposing a tight siege of Hebron amid raids, home demolitions and displacement.
articles.body:
The Israeli army is continuing its military lockdown of Hebron for the seventh consecutive day, carrying out raids and tightening restrictions in the occupied West Bank’s largest city.

Two Palestinians were injured and seven detained by Israeli forces on Thursday, according to the Wafa news agency, as Israeli settlers attacked Palestinians and their vehicles in the Ras al-Joura area, near the city’s northern entrance.

Israel has imposed a tight siege of Hebron since Friday last week, closing all entrances and exits and restricting residents’ freedom of movement and their ability to access critical services. More than 3,000 people have been forced out of the city as a number of Palestinian homes have been converted into military posts and barracks .

Meanwhile, Israeli settlers carried out attacks on Palestinian communities around Hebron. In the latest incident on Wednesday, settlers assaulted three foreign journalists, Andrey Ilyich Khrzhanovskiy, also known as Andrey X, Adele Shoko and Jasper Nathaniel. Andrey X reportedly lost consciousness, was taken to a police station and remained detained without receiving medical care.

What has happened over the past week in Hebron?

Israel’s campaign follows the killing of two Israeli soldiers by Palestinian gunmen at a checkpoint near the illegal Israeli settlement of Telem last week. The gunmen were later killed by Israeli forces in Hebron.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced on social media that he had ordered security forces to immediately close Hebron and “prepare for a full lockdown across all of Judea and Samaria [the Israeli term for the occupied West Bank].

“We will act to destroy this place, to change it completely,” he proclaimed.

Israel’s far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich called for “a comprehensive military campaign in [the West Bank]… exactly as we did in Gaza”. A United Nations inquiry last year found Israel’s war on Gaza constituted a genocide .

As the siege began, Israeli forces launched a large demolition operation on dozens of Palestinian buildings. Troops also stormed the Ein Deir Bahha neighbourhood, forcing dozens of families to flee their homes at night without any belongings.

Footage showed Israeli soldiers beating and injuring Hijazi Shawer, a 70-year-old Palestinian shopkeeper and community leader.

Israeli forces also fired tear gas canisters at Al-Ahli Hospital in Hebron, causing panic among patients and staff. Hospitals are strictly protected under international humanitarian law, but the Israeli military has been known to attack hospitals throughout its genocidal war on Gaza , as well.

On Wednesday, the Palestinian Prisoner’s Society reported that at least 110 people had been detained in the Hebron governorate since the raids began, including three women and seven children.

As Israeli forces besieged Hebron, they also isolated 12 villages and hamlets in the Masafer Yatta region in the south, leaving residents and farmers cut off from urban centres and markets, and dozens of patients who require daily medical care unable to reach hospitals.

Israeli settlers uprooted more than 200 fruit trees, destroyed water wells and agricultural facilities east of Hebron, and prevented farmers from harvesting olives, Wafa reported. Hebron accounts for about 40 percent of Palestinian industrial output and 30 percent of exports.

Israeli forces on Wednesday detained a Palestinian victim of a settler assault in the Khirbet Quwaweis area of Masafer Yatta, south of Hebron. A young man and a woman were also detained in the al-Kassara area, south of Hebron, following an Israeli raid on Monday.

Palestinian officials have accused Netanyahu and his hard-right government of exploiting the operation to secure settler votes before Tuesday’s elections in Israel this week.

Palestinian human rights organisation Al-Haq said the siege of Hebron violates international law and amounts to an international crime. “Given the illegality of Israel’s military occupation and the illegal settler colonial apartheid regime, the entire military operation in Hebron constitutes a prohibited act of aggression,” it stated.

The Israeli NGO B’Tselem said the Israeli military’s “operation in Hebron has nothing to do with security. It is an act of collective punishment.”

UN Human Rights Chief Volker Turk said: “Collective punishment is a grave violation of international law. Threats to empty and erase entire neighbourhoods also raise serious concerns of ethnic cleansing.”

Roland Friedrich, the director of UNRWA Affairs for the occupied West Bank, said the developments brought “alarming echoes of the massive displacement witnessed in the northern occupied West Bank in early 2025, where more than 34,000 Palestine refugees from Jenin, Tulkarem and Nur Shams camps remain forcibly displaced over a year later”.

Muhammed Shehada, at the Euro-Med Human Rights Monitor, told Al Jazeera that the Israeli government’s use of collective punishment as a tool of deterrence against Palestinians has reached unprecedented levels.

“It’s not just about punishing the family [of an attacker], but it’s about punishing the entire community, the whole neighbourhood, the whole town and even the whole city,” he said.

Shehada argued that the genocide in Gaza had turned previously “unthinkable” policies into “core tactics”. “The Israeli government’s goal is to advance de facto annexation, ethnic cleansing in the West Bank by making life impossible,” he said.

In this context, Shehada added, collective punishment should be seen as “a terror tactic” to prevent any reaction to the unprecedented pace of ethnic cleansing and displacement of the Palestinian population.

articles.title: Why is Russia sending fighter jets and air defences to Ethiopia?
articles.summary: Experts say Moscow is seeking arms revenue and further diplomatic influence.
articles.body:
Ethiopia has received 12 Russian Su-35 fighter jets and will acquire four S-400 air defence batteries, in a deal experts say strengthens Moscow’s foothold in the Horn of Africa while bolstering Addis Ababa’s military amid conflict at home and tensions with neighbouring Eritrea.

Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed announced the deal in Moscow during the two-day Russia-Africa Summit .

“I value the friendly relations between Russia and Ethiopia,” Russian President Vladimir Putin said in a statement. “Russia and Ethiopia stand together in international affairs.”

Experts say the agreement builds on decades of military cooperation, offering Moscow arms revenue and diplomatic influence while allowing Ethiopia to strengthen its armed forces amid its ongoing conflict in Tigray.

Abiy said Ethiopia had taken delivery of its first 12 Su-35s under an earlier agreement with Russia, with four S-400 batteries to follow, but did not say when the air defence systems would arrive.

The aircraft would expand an air force already equipped with Russian fighter jets. The S-400 systems would complement this existing fleet by helping the military defend itself against aerial threats, experts say.

“They would be best used against conventional air threats,” Benedict Manzin, a lead analyst on the Middle East and Africa at risk consultancy Sibylline, told Al Jazeera. “In a war with Eritrea, they could be used against Eritrea’s limited air force and drones.”

However, air defences do not provide protection against every kind of attack.

“As we have seen in Ukraine, conventional air defence systems can be overwhelmed by small, cheap drones,” he said.

Why does Russia want closer ties with Ethiopia?

The relationship predates the current competition for influence in Africa.

“Russia has been engaged in Ethiopia for decades, part of the legacy of the Cold War,” Manzin said.

The Soviet Union backed Ethiopia’s former communist government. Today’s cooperation builds on those foundations, with the two countries having signed military agreements intended to improve the Ethiopian armed forces’ capabilities through technology, knowledge and training, according to the Ethiopian News Agency.

“Russia is also in the business of making money through arms sales,” Manzin said. “This is one of Russia’s primary exports to Africa.”

Weapons sales provide revenue while sustaining relationships with governments that require training, maintenance and replacement equipment. But the partnership extends beyond defence.

Abiy said his talks with Putin covered nuclear energy, health and trade, alongside bilateral and multilateral cooperation, while in a statement, Putin said bilateral trade exceeded $1.3bn in January-September, more than twice the figure for all of 2025.

He identified energy, agriculture, industry and education among potential areas for further cooperation.

Ethiopia’s size also makes it attractive to competing powers, with experts saying that because it is Africa’s second-most populous country, it offers a substantial market.

“Everyone engages a bit, and Ethiopia tries to maximise its gains,” Manzin said.

Does this mean Ethiopia is turning away from the West?

Manzin suggested Ethiopia is widening its options rather than committing exclusively to Moscow.

“African states are aware that they are a focus of geopolitical competition,” he said.

That competition gives governments room to seek weapons, investment and diplomatic backing from different partners. Ethiopia’s relationship with Russia coexists with a significant Chinese presence and continuing Western investment in the country.

“China has a huge presence in Ethiopia, and Russian arms have always been a huge factor,” Manzin said. Moscow is seeking to turn those established connections into broader influence as Western sanctions over its war in Ukraine constrain its international relationships.

Russia supplied 15 percent of African imports of major weapons in 2021–2025, behind the United States at 19 percent and China at 17 percent, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI).

In his statement, Abiy thanked Putin for ensuring the aircraft were delivered a year ahead of schedule and said the equipment would strengthen Ethiopia’s ability to “preemptively deter aggression”.

The delivery comes amid renewed fighting in Tigray, a separate rebellion in Amhara and concerns about a possible conflict with Eritrea.

“Ethiopia is buying a lot of aircraft,” Manzin said. “The timing comes as Ethiopia is going through conflict in Tigray, with speculation about war with Eritrea.”

He cautioned against assuming the latest battlefield developments directly prompted purchases negotiated earlier.

“Aircraft are helpful regardless, as they are using aircraft and the air force heavily during any suppression,” he said.

Fighting between Ethiopia’s federal army and Tigrayan forces intensified in late September, in effect unravelling the November 2022 Pretoria peace agreement that ended a devastating two-year war.

Each side has blamed the other for renewed violence. Tensions grew following the formation of a seven-group alliance seeking to overthrow Abiy’s government and establish a transitional administration.

Government troops and allied forces entered Mekelle, Tigray’s capital, earlier in October after Tigray People’s Liberation Front ( TPLF ) fighters withdrew.

Addis Ababa subsequently installed a six-month caretaker administration, but rebel commanders have promised to continue fighting.

articles.title: FIR against two education dept employees for siphoning off Rs 60L
articles.summary: FIR filed against two East Champaran education dept employees for allegedly siphoning Rs 60 lakh via HRMS salary system; police probe continues, accused absconding.
articles.body: Motihari: An FIR has been lodged against two employees of the East Champaran education department for allegedly siphoning off around Rs 60 lakh by manipulating the Human Resource Management System (HRMS) used for salary payments to teachers and non-teaching staff.District education officer (DEO) Rajan Kumar Giri said the irregularities came to light during a special probe ordered by the education department. The investigation found that funds meant for salaries were allegedly diverted to personal and family members’ bank accounts between June 2024 and Sept 2026.The accused have been identified as Mohd Imaduddin Shabir, a teacher who was posted on deputation at the DEO office, and HRMS operator Aman Kumar. Police said the duo are absconding and a reward of Rs 10,000 each has been announced for information leading to their arrest.According to the probe, the allegedly misappropriated funds were transferred to accounts linked to the accused persons’ family members. Police are also examining possible lapses in the DEO office’s verification and bill-processing system. articles.title: Russian drone attack on Ukrainian train station kills at least 13, officials say
articles.body:
Thirteen people have been killed after a Russian jet-powered drone hit a crowded platform at Dnipro railway station in the country's north, Ukrainian officials have said.

Dnipropetrovsk regional head Oleksandr Hanzha said at least 10 others were wounded in the attack, including an 11-year-old boy.

According to the Ukrainian railway operator, Ukrzaliznytsia, a train headed for Zaporizhzhia was at one of the platforms in Dnipro when the drone hit.

Moscow has repeatedly targeted Ukraine's large railway network but it denies deliberately targeting civilians.

Elsewhere in Ukraine, two girls aged 15 were killed in a Russian missile attack on the centre of Chernihiv city, in the north of the country, regional head Vyacheslav Chaus said. At least 11 others, including more children, were injured, he added.

In Dnipro, an elevated threat level was announced ahead of Thursday's strike, according to Ukraine Railways head Oleksandr Pertsovsky.

"But unfortunately there were still a large number of people on the platform," he said.

Dnipro Mayor Borys Filatov said the incident was a tragedy, adding that a drone hit a civilian electric train.

Pictures from the Ukrainian rescue services show a large hole ripped in a platform strewn with blurred-out bodies, near a blast-damaged train with smashed windows.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said "the Russians used a drone to attack a platform where a regular commuter train and a regular passenger train were standing."

He called for further US, European and G7 sanctions on Russia following the incident and repeated his criticism of a controversial deal struck earlier this month between Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin, which eased some sanctions on Russia, allowing the US to import Russian diesel.

Russia's defence ministry denies targeting Ukrainian civilians and says its attacks on railways target the infrastructure used to transport military personnel and equipment.

However, the dangers to passengers are very real. Attacks on Ukraine's rolling stock and stations have risen sharply.

Of the 521 locomotives hit since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion, almost 60% have been his this year, according to statistics released by Ukrzaliznytsia supplied to AFP news agency. Overall attacks on railway facilities have risen from 1,206 in 2025 to 1,700 so far this year.

There appears to have been a wider assault on Ukraine's infrastructure in recent weeks, with two bridges attacked in Kyiv, and a metro train hit during one of the strikes.
